Specification

Complete Language Specification

The complete compiler-verified Lora Language Reference (docs/language.md — all 27 sections from Programs through Defined Behaviour and Omitted Features).

Lora is a statically typed systems language. It compiles ahead of time through QBE to native code for macOS and Linux (arm64 and x86_64), calls C directly, and has no garbage collector. This document describes the language as the Lora compiler implements it today: what each feature does, examples you can copy, and where each feature stops.

Every lora example below is checked against the compiler by scripts/check-doc-examples.py. Examples marked // error: … show code the compiler rejects, with the start of its message. Examples marked // aborts compile but stop the program at run time.

For which features to reach for, and how to write Lora that is memory safe, robust and fast, see Idiomatic Lora.

1. Programs

A program is a list of declarations. It starts at export fn main, which takes no parameters and returns void:

lora 
use fmt;
use strings;

export fn main() void = {
	let greeting = strings::concat("hello", ", world")!;
	defer free(greeting);
	fmt::println(greeting)!;
}
sh 
lora run hello.lora          # build and run
lora build -o hello hello.lora
lora check hello.lora        # type-check only
  • use statements come first, before any other declaration.
  • A program can span several files: lora build -o app a.lora b.lora. The files share one namespace.
  • Command-line arguments come from os::args, the exit status from os::exit(n).
lora 
fn helper() void = void;
use fmt; // error: syntax error: expected 'const', 'let', 'def', 'type', 'fn', found 'use'
export fn main() void = void;

2. Lexical structure

Comments start with // and run to the end of the line. There are no block comments. A comment directly above a declaration is its documentation, which the editor shows on hover.

Identifiers start with a letter or _ and go on with letters, digits and _, in any script: Unicode letters (categories L and Nl) start them, and combining marks, digits and connectors (Mn, Mc, Nd, Pc) may follow, as in UAX #31. Qualified names use ::: fmt::println, color::green.

lora 
type größe = struct { breite: int, höhe: int }
const π: f64 = 3.14159;

fn fläche(g: größe) int = g.breite * g.höhe;

export fn main() void = {
	let café = größe { breite = 3, höhe = 4 }
	let 名前 = "Lora";
	assert(fläche(café) == 12 && π > 3.0 && 名前 == "Lora");
}

Symbols in object files are ASCII: a name's characters beyond ASCII are written _U<hex>_ (café is caf_UE9_), so C code calling an exported Lora function with such a name uses that spelling.

lora 
export fn main() void = {
	let x€ = 1; // error: syntax error: unexpected codepoint
}

Semicolons end statements and declarations. One that would come right after the } ending a statement or declaration may be left out: an if, for or match, a block, a struct literal, a function whose body is a block, a type, an impl, a use with {...}.

lora 
use fmt;

type point = struct {
	x: int,
	y: int,
}

fn sum(xs: []int) int = {
	let n = 0;
	for (let x .. xs) {
		n += x;
	}
	return n;
}

export fn main() void = {
	let p = point { x = 1, y = 2 }
	if (sum([p.x, p.y]) == 3) {
		fmt::println("three")!;
	}
}

What comes after such a } begins the next statement, unless it goes on with this one on the same line (} else {, }.x, } as t) or with an operator. A line that starts with (, [ or * right after a } could be either, so it is an error until the statement before is ended with ;:

lora 
export fn main() void = {
	let n = 0;
	let p = &n;
	let q = point { x = 1, y = 2 }
	*p = 2; // error: syntax error: This line starts with *, which would go on with the statement that ended with } on line 4. If it starts a new statement, end that one with ; after its }.
}

The formatter takes out the ; after such a }, and keeps it where the next line needs it.

Keywords (reserved everywhere):

text 
_ abort align alloc append as assert bool break const continue def defer
delete done else enum export f32 f64 false fn for free i16 i32 i64 i8 if
insert int is len let match never nomem null nullable offset opaque ref
return rune size static str struct true type u16 u32 u64 u8 uint uintptr
union use usize vaarg vaend valist vastart void yield

macro, closure, interface and impl are special only where they start a declaration or a type, and requires and ensures only after a function's result type (unit functions), so they remain usable as names:

lora 
let interface = 1, impl = 2, closure = 3, macro = 4, requires = 5, ensures = 6;
assert(interface + impl + closure + macro + requires + ensures == 21);

Literals

lora 
let dec = 1_000_000;          // `_` separates digits
let hex = 0xff, oct = 0o17, bin = 0b1010;
let byte = 0xffu8;            // suffixes: i8 i16 i32 i64 u8 u16 u32 u64 u (uint) z (usize)
let n = 10z;                  // size
let f = 1.5, g = 2.0f32;      // f64 unless suffixed
let e = 1.5e3;                // 1500.0
let r = 'λ';                  // rune: a Unicode scalar value
let s = "tab\there\n";        // escapes: \n \t \r \0 \\ \" \' \xNN \uNNNN \UNNNNNNNN
let raw = `C:\no\escapes`;    // raw string, may span lines
let joined = "ab" "cd";       // adjacent literals are joined: "abcd"
assert(joined == "abcd" && len(raw) == 13);

An unsuffixed integer literal has no fixed type until it is used: it takes the type its context needs, and int when nothing says otherwise. It must fit that type:

lora 
let x: u8 = 300; // error: The constant 300 does not fit in u8

Limit: an exponent without a decimal point makes an integer literal: 1e3 is the integer 1000, and 1e308 overflows. Write 1.0e308 for a float.

lora 
let x = 1e3;
let i: int = x;        // an integer
assert(i == 1000);

3. Types

Built-in types

TypeSize (bytes)Notes
i8 i16 i32 i641 2 4 8signed, two's complement
u8 u16 u32 u641 2 4 8unsigned
int uint432-bit on every supported platform
usize8lengths and indices (len returns usize)
uintptr8an integer that can hold a pointer
f32 f644 8IEEE 754
bool1true, false
rune4a Unicode scalar value
str24UTF-8 bytes: pointer, length, capacity
void0no value
never—the type of expressions that do not return (abort, return)
done0the value that ends an iterator
nomem0the out-of-memory error
opaque—unknown contents; only behind pointers
valist—a C variadic argument list
lora 
assert(size_of(int) == 4 && size_of(usize) == 8 && size_of(str) == 24);

Use usize for lengths and indices and i64/u64 when a value needs 64 bits; int overflows at about ±2.1 billion.

A rune is a character, not a number.

  • Ordered by code point: <, <=, > and >= order runes by code point, as ranges and patterns of them ('a'..='z') do. So 'Z' comes before 'a', and 'é' (U+00E9) after 'z'.
  • No arithmetic: to compute with a rune's number, convert it with @u32, and back with @rune.
lora 
let r = 'g';
assert('a' <= r && r <= 'z');
assert('Z' < 'a' && 'é' > 'z');
let next = @rune(@u32(r) + 1);
assert(next == 'h');
lora 
let r = 'a' + 1; // error: Cannot combine a flexible rune and the constant 1

Pointers

FormMeaning
*Ta pointer that is never null
nullable *Ta pointer that may be null; must be checked before use
*const Ta pointer through which T is not changed (for C)
*opaquea pointer to anything (like C's void *)
*[*]Ta pointer to an array of unknown length; can be indexed, unchecked
lora 
type point = struct { x: int, y: int }

export fn main() void = {
	let p = point { x = 1, y = 2 }
	let ptr = &p;
	ptr.x = 10;                 // fields are reached through pointers directly
	assert((*ptr).x == 10 && p.x == 10);

	let maybe: nullable *point = null;
	assert(maybe == null);
	maybe = ptr;                // *T converts to nullable *T
	let sure = maybe as *point; // checked: aborts if null
	assert(sure.y == 2);

	let a = [1, 2, 3];
	let many: *[*]int = &a;     // no bounds checks through *[*]T,
	assert(unsafe { many[2] } == 3); // so indexing it is unsafe
}

A nullable pointer cannot be dereferenced until it has been checked, with match, if let, as or ??:

lora 
let p: nullable *int = null;
let v = *p; // error: Cannot dereference a nullable pointer
lora 
let p: *int = null; // error: Initializer of type null is not assignable to binding type *int

Pointer arithmetic moves a pointer by whole elements: p + n, n + p, p - n, p += n, p++. The distance between two pointers of the same type, p - q, is an element count of type i64, and pointers can be ordered with <, <=, > and >=. Nothing is bounds-checked, so it is unsafe: keep pointers inside the array they point into (slices and indexing are checked, and are usually the better choice).

lora 
type pt = struct { x: i64, y: i64 }

export fn main() void = unsafe {
	let a = [10, 20, 30, 40];
	let p = &a[0];
	let q = p + 2;                    // two ints along
	assert(*q == 30 && *(q - 1) == 20 && q - p == 2);
	p += 3;
	p--;
	assert(*p == 30 && p > &a[0]);
	let pts = [pt { x = 1, y = 2 }, pt { x = 3, y = 4 }];
	let second = &pts[0] + 1;         // moves by size_of(pt) bytes
	assert(second.x == 3);
}

Arithmetic needs a non-nullable pointer to something with a size, and cannot add two pointers:

lora 
let a = 1;
let o: *opaque = &a;
let o2 = o + 1; // error: Cannot do arithmetic on this pointer: what it points to has no size
lora 
let a = 1;
let n: nullable *int = &a;
let m = n + 1; // error: Cannot do arithmetic on this pointer: a nullable pointer may be null

Partial borrows

A view, *T.{fields}, is a pointer to a struct or union through which only the fields it names can be reached: a borrow of part of a value. const before a field lets it be read but not changed, and *const T.{a, b} is *T.{const a, const b}. A pointer to the whole converts to a view implicitly, and a view to a view of fewer fields; &x.{fields} names the view where it is taken.

lora 
type foo = struct { a: usize, b: u32, label: str }

fn increment_b(f: *foo.{b}) void = {
	f.b += 1;
}

fn total(f: *foo.{const a, const b}) usize = f.a + @usize(f.b);

export fn main() void = {
	let x = foo { a = 101, b = 42, label = "x" }
	let a = &x.a;
	increment_b(&x);         // &x is *foo; it narrows to *foo.{b}
	*a += 1;                 // the call could not reach x.a
	increment_b(&x.{b});     // the view, named
	assert(x.a == 102 && x.b == 44 && total(&x) == 146);
}

Through a view, other fields cannot be read or changed, the whole value cannot be dereferenced or passed on as *T, and const fields cannot be changed. @*T(view) converts back explicitly, outside these rules.

lora 
type foo = struct { a: usize, b: u32 }

fn peek(f: *foo.{b}) usize = f.a; // error: `a` is not part of the view *foo.{b}: a view reaches only the fields it names
fn grab(f: *foo.{b}) *foo = f; // error: Expression result type *foo.{b} is not assignable to function result type *foo
fn reset(f: *foo.{const b}) void = { f.b = 0; } // error: Cannot change this: the view it is reached through has 'const b'
export fn main() void = void;

A view promises its callee that the fields it names are reached no other way during the call, so one call cannot also pass a pointer that reaches one of them, if either can change it. Disjoint fields are fine:

lora 
type foo = struct { a: usize, b: u32 }

fn both(f: *foo.{b}, a: *usize) void = { f.b += 1; *a += 1; }
fn twice(f: *foo.{b}, b: *u32) void = void;

export fn main() void = {
	let x = foo { a = 1, b = 2 }
	both(&x, &x.a);   // x.b and x.a: disjoint
	twice(&x, &x.b); // error: Arguments 1 and 2 both reach 'x.b', and one can change it
}

An interface method can take a view of its receiver, as in fn step(c: *counter.{n}) void, so it is known to change only n.

Arrays

[N]T is a fixed-size array. It is a value: assigning or passing it copies all its elements. [_]T takes the length from the initializer, and [v...] fills the rest of an array with v:

lora 
let a: [_]int = [1, 2, 3];            // [3]int
let zeros: [64]u8 = [0...];
let grid: [3][3]int = [[0...]...];    // arrays of arrays
grid[1][2] = 5;
let b = a;                            // a copy
b[0] = 99;
assert(a[0] == 1 && len(a) == 3 && grid[1][2] == 5);
let c: [len(a)]int = [0...];          // len of an array is a constant
assert(len(c) == 3);

Indexing is bounds-checked. A constant index past the end is a compile error, any other one aborts at run time:

lora 
let a = [1, 2, 3];
let x = a[5]; // error: Index must be less than the array's length
lora 
// aborts
let a = [1, 2, 3];
let i = 5z;
let x = a[i];     // slice or array access out of bounds

Slices

[]T is a view of an array: a pointer, a length and a capacity. Slicing (a[lo..hi], either end optional) makes a view that shares the elements:

lora 
let a = [1, 2, 3, 4];
let s = a[1..3];      // [2, 3]
s[0] = 20;
assert(a[1] == 20 && len(s) == 2);
let all = a[..];
let tail = a[2..];
assert(len(all) == 4 && tail[0] == 3);

Slices that own heap memory are grown with append and insert, shrunk with delete and released with free (see Memory).

A slice is a span: it views elements it does not own, and the compiler tracks what it points into, so a view never outlives its array (L0608). Three forms say more about what a view may do:

FormWhat it is
[]const Ta view that only reads: no assigning, & gives *const T, no append or delete
@*[n]T(s)a view of exactly n elements, checked once: indexing it needs no more checks
at(s, i)element i of a slice or array as a pointer, or null when there is none

[]T and arrays pass where []const T is wanted, and not the other way:

lora 
fn total(xs: []const int) int = {
	let t = 0;
	for (let x .. xs) t += x;
	return t;
}

export fn main() void = {
	let v = [1, 2, 3, 4];
	assert(total(v) == 10 && total(v[1..]) == 9);
	let four = @*[4]int(v[..]);       // aborts unless len is 4
	four[0] = 7;
	assert(v[0] == 7);
	match (at(v, 9)) {
		let p: *int => *p = 0,
		null => void,                     // no element 9: handled, not a stop
	}
}
lora 
let xs: []const int = [1, 2];
xs[0] = 1; // error: Cannot change this: it is an element of a []const slice.
lora 
let xs: []const int = [1, 2];
let p = @*[2]int(xs); // error: A []const slice is only read through, and so is a view of it.

A view of a []const T is @*const [n]T(s), and at on one gives nullable *const T. Returning at(a, i) or @*[n]T(a) of a local array is L0608, as returning a[..] is.

Strings

A str is UTF-8 bytes. len(s) counts bytes. Strings compare with == and !=, and the strings module does everything else:

lora 
use strings;

export fn main() void = {
	let s = "héllo";
	assert(len(s) == 6);                         // bytes, not characters
	assert(strings::runecount(s) == 5);
	assert(s == "héllo" && s != "hello");
	let bytes = strings::to_bytes(s);
	assert(bytes[0] == @u8('h'));
	let up = strings::toupper(s)!;
	defer free(up);
	assert(strings::has_prefix(up, "H"));
}

s[a..b] is the bytes a to b of a string, as a str that borrows them: no copy is made. A bound may not fall inside a character, which would leave invalid UTF-8: that is a compile error for a constant string and bounds, and aborts at run time otherwise, saying where.

lora 
export fn main() void = {
	let s = "héllo";
	assert(s[..3] == "hé" && s[3..] == "llo");   // é is two bytes
	let n = 1z;
	assert(s[n..3] == "é");
}
lora 
let s = "héllo"[..2]; // error: This slice 0..2 cuts a character: byte 2 is inside a multi-byte UTF-8 character.

What strings cannot do:

lora 
let s = "abc";
let c = s[0]; // error: Can only index into an array or a slice, but this is str
lora 
let s = "a" + "b"; // error: Cannot do arithmetic on a str
lora 
let lt = "a" < "b"; // error: Cannot order values of a str with <, >, <= or >=

Use strings::to_bytes(s)[i] or strings::at(s, i) for bytes, strings::concat or interpolation to join, and strings::compare to order.

Structs and unions

lora 
type point = struct { x: int, y: int }
type pixel = struct {
	point,              // embedded: its fields become pixel's fields
	color: u32,
}
type header = struct @packed { tag: u8, length: u32 }   // no padding
type bits = union { i: u32, f: f32 }                    // overlapping storage

export fn main() void = {
	let p = point { x = 1, y = 2 }
	let q = point { x = 1, ... }       // `...` zeroes the remaining fields
	let px = pixel { x = 3, y = 4, color = 0xff }
	assert(q.y == 0 && px.x == 3);
	assert(size_of(header) == 5);
	let b = bits { f = 1.0 }
	assert(b.i == 0x3f800000);
}

Layout. A struct or union may say how it is laid out, after its keyword:

AttributeEffect
@packedno padding between fields; its alignment is 1
@align(n)aligned to n, a power of two up to 128: on the stack, the heap and in globals
@field_align(min = n, max = m)each field aligned to at least n, and at most m
@simple== and != compare its bytes
@sealedonly its module reads and writes its fields
@synchronisedits module guards it for threads, and only its module touches its fields
lora 
type line = struct @align(64) { hits: u64 }            // a cache line of its own
type wire = struct @field_align(max = 2) { tag: u8, n: u64 }
type key = struct @simple { a: u32, b: u32 }

export fn main() void = {
	assert(size_of(line) == 64 && size_of(wire) == 10);
	assert(key { a = 1, b = 2 } == key { a = 1, b = 2 });
}

@align(n) can't be less than what the fields need: limit them first with @field_align(max = n). A slice of values aligned beyond 16 can't grow, as memory that grows is aligned to 16: allocate it once, as big as it needs. A @simple type can't have padding, a str or slice (whose bytes say where it points, not what), or a tagged union, and comparing its floats compares their bits.

@sealed keeps a type's fields to the module that declares it: code elsewhere can't read or write them, take the type apart in a pattern, embed it, or make one with a literal that sets fields. It uses the functions the module exports, which keep the fields as they must be: a region's addresses, an allocator's position. Only T { ... }, the type's zero value, may be written anywhere, and the module keeps that value good for its functions. @synchronised seals a type too.

lora 
use expanse;

export fn main() void = {
	let r = expanse::auto();
	r.next = 0; // error: `next` is a field of expanse::region, which is @sealed
}

When to seal. Seal a type when its own module's unsafe code trusts its fields: a pointer it follows, a position it copies bytes at, an id it gives to the system, a value only its lock may touch. Without the seal, safe code elsewhere could set such a field and the unsafe code would go wrong. A module with no unsafe code needs no seals, as what its fields hold can't break memory safety; nor does a field the unsafe code checks before it uses it. In the library, these are sealed:

ModuleSealed typesWhat their module trusts
allocator, scratchthe allocators, framebuffers and positions it hands memory out of
expanseregion, mark, arraya region's addresses
poolpool, iteratorslot links and the pool's id
rc, arcrc, weak, arccounts and the pointer they guard
corochan, case, waitq, group, scope, results, serial, arrivalsa channel's ring, a case's channel, the scheduler's queues
threadthread, mutex, cond, atomic, shareda thread's id, a lock's state, values reached only atomically or under a lock

Each one's zero value, T { ... }, is ready to use.

A union keeps no record of which field was written last. Reading a field of numbers is a reinterpretation, and safe; reading one that holds a pointer, a view, a bool or an enum needs unsafe, as its bits may not be one. A union can't hold an owner: nothing could tell whether to drop it. A tagged union, (T | U), knows which it holds.

Field defaults. A field can have a default, name: T = value, used when a struct literal leaves the field out. Fields without one must be given, unless the literal ends with ..., which zero-fills them:

lora 
type config = struct {
	host: str = "localhost",
	port: u16 = 8080,
	verbose: bool,
}

type inner = struct { depth: int = 7 }
type outer = struct { inner, name: str = "outer" }   // embedded defaults apply too

export fn main() void = {
	let a = config { verbose = true }            // host and port from defaults
	let b = config { port = 9000, verbose = false }
	let c = outer { ... }
	assert(a.host == "localhost" && a.port == 8080 && b.port == 9000);
	assert(c.depth == 7 && c.name == "outer");
}
  • A default must be known at compile time (a literal, a constant, or @comptime(...)), and of the field's type.
  • Defaults are part of the struct type, and they cross module boundaries with it.
  • Union members cannot have defaults.
lora 
type config = struct { port: u16 = "80" } // error: The default of `port` is a str, but the field is a u16
export fn main() void = void;
lora 
fn compute() int = 3;
type config = struct { n: int = compute() } // error: The default of `n` must be known while compiling: it is written into each literal that leaves the field out
export fn main() void = void;
lora 
type config = struct { host: str = "x", verbose: bool }
export fn main() void = {
	let c = config { host = "y" } // error: `verbose` has no value in this literal, and a struct's fields all need one
}

Structs are values, copied on assignment. Two struct values cannot be compared with ==:

lora 
type point = struct { x: int, y: int }
fn same(a: point, b: point) bool = a == b; // error: Cannot compare struct values with == or !=
export fn main() void = void;

Tagged unions

(A | B | C) holds a value of exactly one of its member types and knows which. is tests the member and as extracts it (aborting if it is the wrong one); match handles every case:

lora 
type token = (int | str | void);

fn describe(t: token) str = match t {
	let n: int => if (n < 0) "negative" else "number",
	let s: str => s,
	void => "nothing",
}

export fn main() void = {
	let t: token = 42;
	assert(t is int && t as int == 42);
	assert(describe("word") == "word" && describe(void) == "nothing");
	let nested: (int | (str | bool)) = true;   // nested unions flatten
	assert(nested is bool);
	let wider: (int | str | bool) = t as int;
	assert(wider is int);
}

Operators don't apply to a tagged union itself, since it may hold a member they make no sense for: take the member out first.

lora 
let r: (int | void) = 5;
let big = r > 0; // error: Cannot compare (void | int), a tagged union
let ok = r is int && r as int > 0;

A union converts to a union with more members, but not to one member or a smaller union without a check:

lora 
let t: (int | str) = 1;
let n: int = t; // error: Initializer of type (str | int) is not assignable to binding type int
lora 
// aborts
let t: (int | str) = 5;
let s = t as str;     // type assertion failed

Tagged unions, like tuples and arrays, cannot be compared with ==. Match on them instead.

Tuples

lora 
fn divmod(a: int, b: int) (int, int) = (a / b, a % b);

export fn main() void = {
	let t = divmod(7, 2);
	assert(t.0 == 3 && t.1 == 1);
	let (q, r) = divmod(9, 4);
	let (_, rest) = divmod(9, 4);
	assert(q == 2 && r == 1 && rest == 1);
}

Named parts. A tuple's parts can be named in its type, so that a signature says what each is, and read by name, t.quot, as well as by number. A tuple is made with names, (quot = 3, rem = 1), or by position where the type is known:

lora 
fn divmod(a: int, b: int) (quot: int, rem: int) = (quot = a / b, rem = a % b);

fn bounds(xs: []int) (lo: int, hi: int) = {
	let lo = xs[0], hi = xs[0];
	for (let x .. xs) {
		if (x < lo) lo = x;
		if (x > hi) hi = x;
	}
	return (lo, hi);                    // by position: the type names them
}

export fn main() void = {
	let d = divmod(7, 2);
	assert(d.quot == 3 && d.rem == 1 && d.0 == 3);
	let b = bounds([3, 9, 1]);
	assert(b.lo == 1 && b.hi == 9);
	let plain: (int, int) = d;          // the same parts, unnamed
	let (q, r) = divmod(9, 4);          // unpacked as any tuple
	assert(plain.0 == 3 && q == 2 && r == 1);
}

A named tuple and an unnamed one of the same parts take each other; two whose parts are named differently don't, as their parts mean different things: (x: int, y: int) is not a (quot: int, rem: int). A tuple names all its parts or none, and no name twice. @all names its results the same way: let r = @all(user = load(id), orders = count(id))?; gives r.user and r.orders.

Patterns in let and for. What a let or a for binds can be a pattern, taking a value apart: tuples nested in tuples, a tuple's named parts in any order, a struct by its fields' names, and .. for the parts left out:

lora 
type point = struct { x: int, y: int }

fn divmod(a: int, b: int) (quot: int, rem: int) = (quot = a / b, rem = a % b);

export fn main() void = {
	let ((a, b), c) = ((1, 2), 3);
	let point { x, y: height } = point { x = 4, y = 5 }   // x, and y as height
	let (quot = q, ..) = divmod(9, 4);                       // one part, by name
	assert(a + b + c == 6 && x == 4 && height == 5 && q == 2);

	let scores = [("ada", 3), ("bob", 5)];
	let total = 0;
	for (let (name, score) .. scores) total += score;
	let pts = [point { x = 1, y = 2 }, point { x = 3, y = 4 }];
	for (let point { x, .. } .. pts) total += x;
	assert(total == 12);
}

A let always takes its value apart, so its pattern holds names, _ and .., never values to compare: those go in a match. A struct pattern names every field, or ends with ..; a tuple pattern names its parts all by name or all by position. Owners move into their names: a part that owns memory can't be left with _ or .., as it would be dropped unused, and a type that cleans up when dropped (impl drop) can't be taken apart. A static let unpacks a flat tuple only.

Enums

An enum is a type of named values, stored as an integer (or rune). The default storage is int, numbered from 0; a value can be set explicitly, also from the values before it, and the next ones count on from it:

lora 
type color = enum { red, green, blue }
type mode = enum u8 { READ = 1, WRITE, EXEC = 4, ALL = READ + WRITE + EXEC }
type letter = enum rune { A = 'a', B = 'b' }

export fn main() void = {
	assert(@int(color::green) == 1);
	assert(@u8(mode::WRITE) == 2 && @u8(mode::ALL) == 7 && size_of(mode) == 1);
	assert(@rune(letter::B) == 'b');
}

Enums are scoped: a value is named through its enum, color::green, so two enums can both have a red, and neither puts names in the module. Where the enum is already known, .green is enough: a typed binding, an argument, a return, a field, an array element, an assignment, the other side of ==, and a match arm.

lora 
type direction = enum { north, south, east, west }

fn turn(d: direction) direction = match (d) {
	.north => .east,
	.east => .south,
	.south => .west,
	.west => .north,
}

export fn main() void = {
	let d: direction = .north;
	assert(turn(d) == .east && d != .south);
}

Each of the other places, in one program:

lora 
type direction = enum { north, south, east, west }
type robot = struct { name: str, facing: direction }

fn back(d: direction) direction = {
	if (d == .north) return .south;              // == and a return
	return .north;
}

export fn main() void = {
	let d: direction = .east;                    // a typed binding
	let r = robot { name = "r2", facing = .north } // a field
	r.facing = .west;                            // an assignment
	let ways: [2]direction = [.north, .south];   // an array element
	assert(back(.north) == .south);              // an argument
	assert(r.facing == .west && d != .south && ways[1] == .south);
}

An enum is its own type, not a number. Its values compare with ==, != and the orderings, against its own values only, and nothing else: no arithmetic, and no mixing with integers or other enums. Converting is explicit both ways. @int(e) gives the number. @color(n) gives the enum, and checks that n is one of its values: a constant when compiling, anything else when the program runs, which stops if it isn't one. n is color tests first, for a number that may not be one. In @unchecked code the check is left out.

lora 
type color = enum { red, green, blue }

fn parse(n: int) (color | void) = if (n is color) @color(n) else void;

export fn main() void = {
	let n = 2;
	assert(@color(n) == color::blue && @int(color::blue) == 2);
	assert(parse(7) is void);
}
lora 
type color = enum { red, green, blue }
export fn main() void = { let n: int = color::green; } // error: Initializer of type color is not assignable to binding type int
lora 
type color = enum { red, green, blue }
export fn main() void = { let c: color = 1; } // error: A color is one of its named values, and a number is not one of them.
lora 
type color = enum { red, green, blue }
export fn main() void = { let c = @color(7); } // error: 7 is not a value of color.
lora 
type color = enum { red, green, blue }
export fn main() void = { let c = .red; } // error: `.red` is a value of an enum, and nothing here says which enum.
lora 
type name = enum str { A = "a" } // error: syntax error: Enum storage must be an integer or rune
export fn main() void = void;

Enums carry no data. For values with payloads, use a tagged union of structs.

Pattern types

A pattern type is a type whose values also match a pattern: type errno = u32 is 0..4096; is a u32 from 0 to 4095. It has exactly the layout and calling convention of u32, so it costs nothing at run time, and the pattern is checked where values come in. It generalizes NonZero (u32 is 1..) and NonNull (Lora's *T is already never null). A pattern is literals, ranges and constants of an integer or rune type, joined with |; lo.. is a range with no end.

lora 
type errno = u32 is 0..4096;
type nonzero = u32 is 1..;
type digit = rune is '0'..='9';
def MAX: int = 100;
type percent = int is 0..=MAX;
type small_prime = u8 is 2 | 3 | 5 | 7;

fn describe(e: errno) u32 = e;            // errno to u32: nothing is lost

fn parse_errno(n: u32) (errno | void) = n is errno ? @errno(n) : void;

export fn main() void = {
	let e: errno = 2;                      // a constant: checked when compiling
	let raw: u32 = 17;
	let f = @errno(raw);                    // checked when the program runs
	let sum = e + f;                        // arithmetic gives a u32
	let g = @errno(sum);
	assert(describe(e) == 2 && g == 19);
	assert(parse_errno(5000) is void && size_of(errno) == size_of(u32));
	assert('5' is digit && !('x' is digit) && 3u8 is small_prime);
	let nz: nonzero = 1;
	let p: percent = 100;
	assert(nz == 1 && p == 100);
}
  • A value of a pattern type converts to its base type implicitly. The other way, a constant is checked when compiling; any other value needs @errno(x), which aborts if x does not match, or x is errno, which tests without aborting.
  • Arithmetic on a pattern type gives its base type, since the result may be outside the pattern; assign it back with @errno(...). A pattern type cannot be changed in place (+=, ++).
  • Zero-filling (...) is allowed only when the pattern contains 0.
  • Patterns cross module boundaries with the type.
lora 
type errno = u32 is 0..4096;
export fn main() void = {
	let e: errno = 5000; // error: This value does not match the pattern of errno
}
lora 
// aborts
type errno = u32 is 0..4096;
export fn main() void = {
	let n: u32 = 9000;
	let e = @errno(n);   // value does not match its pattern type
}
lora 
type errno = u32 is 0..4096;
export fn main() void = {
	let e: errno = 1;
	e += 1; // error: A value of the pattern type errno cannot be changed in place
}
lora 
type errno = u32 is 0..4096;
export fn main() void = {
	let n: u64 = 3;
	let e = @errno(n); // error: Convert u64 to u32 first
}

Bits

struct @bits(u16) { ... } packs its fields into an unsigned integer: u8, u16, u32 or u64. It is that integer: the same size, passed and compared as it, and a register file or a wire format can be written as one. Each field takes the bits its type needs, from the lowest bit up in order:

Field typeIts bits
boolone
an enumenough for its values
an integer with a pattern, speed: u8 is 0..8, or a pattern typeenough for its pattern
an integerall of its own

@at(n) before a field places it at bit n, and the fields after it follow on. Bits no field has are kept as they are, and can't be reached.

lora 
type mode = enum { off, low, high }

type status = struct @bits(u8) {
	ready: bool,            // bit 0
	error: bool,            // bit 1
	speed: u8 is 0..8,      // bits 2 to 4
	mode: mode,             // bits 5 and 6
	@at(7) busy: bool,      // bit 7
}

fn faster(s: *status) void = {
	s.speed += 1;
}

export fn main() void = {
	let s = status { ready = true, speed = 5, mode = .high, ... }
	faster(&s);
	assert(s.speed == 6 && s.ready && size_of(status) == 1);
	assert(@u8(s) == 0b0_10_110_0_1); // busy, mode, speed, error, ready
}

A field is read and written as any field is, and the other fields' bits stay as they were. What goes in is checked as a pattern type's values are: a constant when compiling, anything else when it is stored, which stops the program if it doesn't fit, and nothing in @unchecked code. So a field always holds one of its values.

A @bits value compares with == and !=. When every field is a bool it is a set of flags, which also combine with |, & and ^, and ~ flips them. Converting is explicit both ways: @u8(s) gives the integer, and @status(n) checks that each enum and pattern field's bits of n hold one of its values, as @e(n) does for an enum. n is status tests it first.

lora 
type perms = struct @bits(u8) { read: bool, write: bool, exec: bool }
type mode = enum { off, low, high }
type status = struct @bits(u8) { ready: bool, mode: mode }

fn parse(n: u8) (status | void) = if (n is status) @status(n) else void;

export fn main() void = {
	let rw = perms { read = true, ... } | perms { write = true, ... }
	assert(rw.read && rw.write && !rw.exec && (~rw).exec);
	assert(parse(0b101) is status && parse(0b111) is void);
}
lora 
type status = struct @bits(u8) { ready: bool, speed: u8 is 0..8 }
export fn main() void = { let s = status { ready = true, speed = 9 } } // error: 9 does not fit in `speed`, which holds 0..8.
lora 
type status = struct @bits(u8) { ready: bool, speed: u8 is 0..8 }
export fn main() void = { let s = status { ready = true, speed = 1 } let p = &s.speed; } // error: A @bits field is some bits of an integer, so it has no address of its own.
lora 
type status = struct @bits(u8) { a: u8 is 0..16, b: u8 is 0..32 } // error: `b` needs bits 4 to 8, and a u8 has 8.
export fn main() void = void;

Declared types and function types

type name = T; declares a type. Each declaration is a type of its own: Lora's types are nominal, so two declarations are different types even when their definitions are identical. Between two declarations, it takes an explicit @T(x), and a value goes into a tagged union only if its type is a member.

A declaration over a number, a bool, a rune or a string is a newtype: its values are its own, apart from its base's too. meters and int don't mix, in assignments, calls or arithmetic, but by @meters(n) and @int(m); a constant fits it, as it fits any type that holds it (let m: meters = 3, let n: name = "ann"), and two meters add up to a meters. So a distance can't be passed where a count is wanted, or an id where a port is. A declaration over a struct, a union or a tagged union converts implicitly to and from what it is defined as, and type b = a is an a.

lora 
type meters = int;
type seconds = int;

fn speed(d: meters, t: seconds) int = @int(d) / @int(t);

export fn main() void = {
	let d: meters = 100;
	let t: seconds = 20;
	let farther = d + 50;                    // meters, with a constant
	assert(speed(farther, t) == 7);
}
lora 
type meters = int;
type seconds = int;
fn speed(d: meters, t: seconds) int = @int(d) / @int(t);
export fn main() void = { let d: meters = 1; let t: seconds = 1; speed(t, d); } // error: Argument type seconds is not assignable to parameter type meters
lora 
type meters = int;
export fn main() void = { let d: meters = 1; let n: int = 2; let x = d + n; } // error: Cannot combine a meters and an int here

The examples below are of declarations over structures:

lora 
type circle = struct { r: f64 }
type rect = struct { w: f64, h: f64 }
type square = struct { w: f64, h: f64 }
type shape = (circle | rect);

fn area(s: shape) f64 = match s {
	let c: circle => 3.0 * c.r * c.r,
	let r: rect => r.w * r.h,
}

export fn main() void = {
	let s = square { w = 2.0, h = 3.0 }
	assert(area(@rect(s)) == 6.0);          // converted explicitly
	assert(area(@shape(s)) == 6.0);         // to the member defined alike
}
lora 
type rect = struct { w: f64, h: f64 }
type square = struct { w: f64, h: f64 }
type shape = (rect | void);

fn area(s: shape) f64 = 0.0;

export fn main() void = {
	area(square { w = 2.0, h = 3.0 }); // error: Argument type square is not assignable to parameter type shape
}
lora 
type meters = int;
type seconds = int;

fn walk(d: meters) void = void;

export fn main() void = {
	let t: seconds = 10;
	walk(t); // error: Argument type seconds is not assignable to parameter type meters
}

The same goes for pointers: a *square is not a *rect.

A function type is written like a declaration without a body. Function values are pointers to it:

lora 
type celsius = f64;
type binop = fn(a: int, b: int) int;

fn add(a: int, b: int) int = a + b;

export fn main() void = {
	let t: celsius = 21.5;
	let f: *binop = &add;
	assert(f(2, 3) == 5 && t > 21.0);
}

4. Conversions

Numbers never convert implicitly. A u8 is not a u32, an i8 not an int and an f32 not an f64, so a value goes into a variable, an argument, a field or a return of another number type, and is combined with one in arithmetic or a comparison, only by @T(x). A constant is not yet of any type, so it fits every type that holds it: let b: u64 = 3. A shift's count may be any integer: x << n has x's type.

Implicit conversions happen only when no information can be lost and no meaning changes:

  • a declared type over a structure (a struct, a union, a tagged union) to and from what it is defined as; a newtype, a declared type over a number, a bool, a rune or a string (type meters = int), only by @meters(n) and @int(m), as its values are its own: see declared types;
  • *T → nullable *T, and any pointer to *opaque;
  • a member type to a tagged union containing it, and a tagged union to a wider one;
  • a capture-free lambda to a closure, as is a function of the same type, named or as &f (it is wrapped in a lambda that calls it), and a pointer to a type to an interface it implements.
lora 
let small: u8 = 3;
let wide = @u32(small);
let neg: i8 = -1;
let big = @int(neg);
let precise = @f64(1.5f32);
let total = wide + @u32(small) + 2;   // the constant 2 is a u32 here
assert(wide == 3 && big == -1 && precise == 1.5 && total == 8);
lora 
let a: u8 = 3;
let b: u32 = a; // error: Initializer of type u8 is not assignable to binding type u32
lora 
let a: u8 = 3;
let b: u32 = 5;
let c = a + b; // error: Cannot combine a u8 and a u32 here: there is no type both convert to.

Everything else needs an explicit conversion, written @T(value): @int(x), @usize(i), @*u8(p), @(int | str)(v), @color(2). The old form value: T is an error that points to it.

A type whose name is also a built-in form's, as @kind(T) and @sealed(T) are, is converted to by its module's name, which its own module may use too: in a module wire with type kind = enum u8 { ... }, @wire::kind(b) converts a byte to it.

lora 
let a: u8 = 3;
let b: i64 = a; // error: Initializer of type u8 is not assignable to binding type i64
lora 
let a = 3;
let b = a: u8; // error: syntax error: a conversion is written @T(value)
lora 
let i: int = 3;
let f: f64 = i; // error: Initializer of type int is not assignable to binding type f64
lora 
let a: int = 3;
let b: uint = 4;
let c = a + b; // error: Cannot combine an int and a uint here
lora 
let a: u8 = 3;
let b = @i64(a);           // explicit: fine
let f = @int(3.7);         // truncates toward zero: 3
let c = @u32('a');         // 97
let r = @rune(65);         // 'A'
let p = @uintptr(&b);      // a pointer as an integer, and back,
let back = unsafe { @*i64(p) } // which is unsafe
assert(b == 3 && f == 3 && c == 97 && r == 'A' && *back == 3);

Casts between integer types truncate or extend silently. Some casts are never allowed:

lora 
let i = @int(true); // error: A bool can't be converted to an int

The three type operators:

OperatorApplies toResult
@T(x)numbers, pointers, enums, tagged membersconverts; never fails
x as Ttagged unions, nullable pointersT, aborting if x holds something else
x is Ttagged unions, nullable pointersbool

5. Expressions and operators

From tightest to loosest binding:

PrecedenceOperators
postfixf(x) a[i] a[lo..hi] s.field t.0 x? x!; conversions @T(x)
unary-x ~x !x *p &x
type testx as T x is T
multiplicative* / % *%
additive+ - +% -%
shift<< >>
bitwise and&
bitwise xor^
bitwise or|
coalesce??
comparison< <= > >=
equality== !=
logical and&&
logical xor^^
logical or||
assignment= += -= *= /= %= +%= -%= *%= <<= >>= &= |= ^= &&= ||= ^^=

Unlike C, the bitwise operators bind tighter than comparisons, so flags & MASK == 0 means (flags & MASK) == 0:

lora 
assert(1 | 2 == 3);           // (1 | 2) == 3
assert(1 << 2 + 1 == 8);      // 1 << (2 + 1)
assert(true || false && false);
assert(true ^^ false);        // logical xor
assert(~0u8 == 255);

Arithmetic rules. Every operation has one result, the same on every machine, at run time and when constants are folded; none is left to the hardware:

  • Integer overflow aborts: +, -, *, -x and / whose true result does not fit the type stop the program with the values and the type, signed or unsigned (0u32 - 1 overflows too). A constant one is a compile error.
  • +%, -%, *% (and +%=, -%=, *%=) wrap instead (two's complement), for hashes, checksums and random numbers: 255u8 +% 1 == 0.
  • Integer division truncates toward zero, and % takes the sign of the dividend: -7 / 2 == -3, -7 % 2 == -1. Dividing by -1 negates, so i32::MIN / -1 overflows; its remainder is 0.
  • Integer division and remainder by zero abort with the location (a constant zero divisor is a compile error).
  • >> of a signed value fills with its sign (-16 >> 2 == -4); of an unsigned one, with zeros.
  • A shift count must be less than the type's width and not negative: a constant one is checked when compiling (1u32 << 40 is an error), and a variable one at run time, which aborts saying so.
  • A float converted to an integer, @i32(f), saturates: values beyond the type's range become its minimum or maximum, and NaN becomes 0.
  • Arithmetic on two constants is worked out when compiling, exactly, with +, -, *, /, %, &, |, ^, << and >>: its value then decides what it fits, so @u8((4999 * 7) & 0xff) is the constant 177.
  • A suffixed literal must fit its type: 300u8 is an error. Hex, octal and binary literals may give a signed type's bit pattern: 0xFFi8 is -1.
  • Floats follow IEEE 754: 1.0 / 0.0 is infinity.
lora 
// aborts
let a = 0;
let b = 7 / a;     // division by zero
lora 
let a: u32 = 1;
let b = a << 40; // error: Shifting a u32 by 40 shifts every bit out
lora 
let x = 300u8; // error: syntax error: Integer literal 300u8 does not fit its type
lora 
let x: u8 = 255;
x +%= 1;              // wraps: x += 1 would stop the program
assert(x == 0);
let y: i8 = 127;
y +%= 1;
assert(y == -128);
assert(0xcbf29ce484222325u64 *% 0x100000001b3 == 0xaf63bd4c8601b7df);
assert(-7 / 2 == -3 && -7 % 2 == -1);
lora 
let big = 2147483647i32 + 1; // error: Integer overflow: 2147483647 + 1 is out of range for i32
let small: u8 = 200 + 100;   // the constant 300 does not fit in u8: an error too
text 
main.lora:3:12: abort: 255 + 1 is 256, which is out of range for u8 (0 to 255).

++ and -- add or subtract 1, before or after the place: x++, ++x, a[i]--. Like every assignment in Lora they are statements, with no value, so there is no "before or after" ordering to get wrong:

lora 
let i = 0;
i++;
++i;
let counts = [0, 0];
counts[1]--;
for (let k = 0; k < 3; k++) i += k;
assert(i == 5 && counts[1] == -1);
lora 
let i = 0;
let j = i++; // error: An assignment has no value

cond ? a : b is a conditional expression, the same as if (cond) a else b. It binds more loosely than every other operator and groups to the right. A ? directly after a value still propagates an error when no : follows in the same expression:

lora 
type not_found = !void;

fn find(n: int) (int | not_found) = n > 0 ? n : not_found;

fn twice(n: int) (int | not_found) = {
	let v = find(n)?;                 // propagates: no ':' follows
	return v * 2;
}

export fn main() void = {
	let x = 5;
	let sign = x > 0 ? 1 : x < 0 ? -1 : 0;   // x > 0 ? 1 : (x < 0 ? -1 : 0)
	let name = x % 2 == 0 ? "even" : "odd";
	assert(sign == 1 && name == "odd" && twice(4)! == 8);
}

Built-in functions

BuiltinDoes
len(x)elements of an array or slice, bytes of a string (usize)
size_of(T) align(T)a type's size and alignment, in bytes
offset(s.field)a field's byte offset in its struct
alloc(v) alloc(init, n)heap allocation, see Memory
free(x)release a heap pointer, slice, string or closure
append(s, v) insert(s[i], v) delete(s[a..b])grow and shrink slices
cap(s)how many elements a slice (or bytes a string) has room for; an array's length
reserve(s, n)room for n more elements without moving s, (void | nomem)
shrink(s)give back the capacity of s beyond its length
assert(cond) assert(cond, "msg")abort with the location if false
abort() abort("msg")stop the program
vastart() vaarg(ap, T) vaend(ap)C variadic arguments
lora 
type rec = struct { tag: u8, value: int }

export fn main() void = {
	let r = rec { tag = 1, value = 2 }
	assert(size_of(rec) == 8 && align(rec) == 4 && offset(r.value) == 4);

	let xs: ^[]int = [];
	defer free(xs);
	reserve(xs, 100)!;               // one allocation for what follows
	for (let i = 0; i < 100; i += 1) append(xs, i)!;
	assert(len(xs) == 100 && cap(xs) == 100);
	shrink(xs);                      // capacity down to the length
}

When append or insert needs more room, the capacity doubles. A slice with no room yet gets at least 16 bytes of elements (16 u8s, 4 ints), the least the system's allocator hands out anyway, so a short slice built up one element at a time is allocated once. delete gives room back as the slice shrinks, but not below that. reserve and shrink make the capacity exactly what they are asked for.

cap, reserve and shrink are built in unless a declaration of that name is in scope, so a variable called cap still works.

6. Bindings and storage

lora 
let counter: int = 0;              // a global: mutable, zero-cost access
const NAME: str = "lora";          // a global constant
def LIMIT: int = 10 * 2;           // a compile-time constant
@threadlocal let scratch: int = 0; // one copy per thread

fn next_id() int = {
	static let n = 0;              // one copy for the whole program
	n += 1;
	return n;
}

export fn main() void = {
	let x = 1;                     // mutable local, type inferred
	let y: u64 = 2;                // with a type
	let a = 1, b = "two";          // several at once
	let x = x + 1;                 // shadowing: a new binding
	next_id();
	assert(next_id() == 2 && x == 2 && LIMIT == 20);
	let buf: [4096]u8 = @undefined;  // zeroed: its value doesn't matter
	buf[0] = 1;
}
  • let declares a mutable binding; def a constant whose value is known at compile time and which takes no storage.
  • Global and static initializers must be computable at compile time. Call functions with @comptime to compute them:
lora 
fn three() int = 3;
let g: int = three(); // error: This initial value must be known at compile time, and it is not
export fn main() void = void;
lora 
fn three() int = 3;
let g: int = @comptime(three());
export fn main() void = { assert(g == 3); }
  • @undefined says a variable's first value does not matter: it is zeroed, like [0...], so it never holds whatever memory was there. Every variable holds a value of its type, so @undefined is only for a type that zero is a value of: not a *T, an enum or pattern type without zero, a tagged union, or a struct or array holding one (@has_zero(T) says). In unsafe code it vouches that the bytes are written before they are read.
lora 
type color = enum { red = 1, green }

export fn main() void = {
	let c: color = @undefined; // error: A color has no zero value, and @undefined is zero.
}
  • Unused variables are allowed.

const bindings and globals cannot be changed: not assigned, not incremented, and no field or element of them changed, appended to or deleted from. A pointer to something const is a *const T, which allows reading only. A *T converts to *const T freely; the other way takes an explicit @*T(p):

lora 
fn read(p: *const int) int = *p;

export fn main() void = {
	const limit = 10;
	let n = 3;
	assert(read(&limit) == 10 && read(&n) == 3);   // &limit is a *const int
	const pair = (1, 2);
	let sum = pair.0 + pair.1;                       // reading is fine
	assert(sum == 3);
}
lora 
const x = 1;
x = 2; // error: Cannot change this: `x` is const
lora 
const xs = [1, 2, 3];
xs[0] = 9; // error: Cannot change this: `xs` is const
lora 
let a = 1;
let p: *const int = &a;
*p = 2; // error: Cannot change this: it is reached through a *const pointer
lora 
fn bump(p: *int) void = { *p += 1; }
export fn main() void = {
	const b = 5;
	bump(&b); // error: Argument type *const int is not assignable to parameter type *int
}

7. Functions

lora 
fn add(a: int, b: int) int = a + b;              // expression body

fn clamp(x: int, lo: int = 0, hi: int = 100) int = {  // default arguments
	if (x < lo) return lo;
	if (x > hi) return hi;
	return x;
}

fn sum(xs: int...) int = {                       // variadic: xs is a []int
	let total = 0;
	for (let x .. xs) total += x;
	return total;
}

fn fail(msg: str) never = abort(msg);            // never returns

fn fact(n: u64) u64 = if (n <= 1) 1 else n * fact(n - 1);

export fn main() void = {
	assert(add(1, 2) == 3);
	assert(clamp(150) == 100 && clamp(-5) == 0 && clamp(5, 10) == 10);
	assert(sum(1, 2, 3) == 6 && sum() == 0 && sum([4, 5]...) == 9);
	assert(fact(10) == 3628800);
	let f = &add;                                // a function pointer
	assert(f(4, 5) == 9);
}
  • A block body runs statements, each ending in ; (or in }, see Semicolons). It returns with return expr;; there is no implicit last-expression value. A body that is one expression is written = expr;.
  • Every path of a non-void function must return or not return at all (never).
  • Functions may call each other in any order and recursively.
  • Arguments are passed by value; pass a pointer to let the callee change the caller's data.

What functions cannot do:

lora 
fn f() int = { 5 } // error: syntax error: expected ';', found '}'
export fn main() void = void;
lora 
fn f(x: int) int = { if (x > 0) return 1; } // error: Expression result type void is not assignable to function result type int
export fn main() void = void;
lora 
fn f(a: int) int = a;
fn f(a: str) str = a; // error: `f` is declared twice in this module, so a use of it couldn't tell which
export fn main() void = void;
lora 
export fn main() void = {
	fn inner() int = 1; // error: syntax error
}
  • There is no overloading: give functions different names, or write one generic function.
  • Functions cannot be declared inside functions; use a lambda.
  • A function used as a value needs &: let f = &add;.
  • C-style variadics (...) are for calling and implementing C ABI functions; see Calling C.

8. Lambdas and closures

fn(params) result = body is an expression. A lambda that uses nothing from the enclosing function is a plain function pointer, usable wherever a *fn is expected, including by C:

lora 
use sort;

type person = struct { name: str, age: int }

export fn main() void = {
	let people = [person { name = "b", age = 30 }, person { name = "a", age = 20 }];
	sort::sort_by(people, fn(a: person, b: person) bool = a.age < b.age);
	assert(people[0].age == 20);
	let square: *fn(x: int) int = fn(x: int) int = x * x;
	assert(square(4) == 16);
}

A lambda that uses local variables is a closure, of type closure(params) result. The variables it uses are copied into an environment allocated when the closure is made. The closure owns the copies: later changes to the original are not seen, and changes through the closure last between calls.

A closure is an owner. Its environment is freed when it is dropped, like any ^T, and passing it moves it, so whoever it is passed to drops it. To use one again after passing it, pass a copy, @clone(f), or a pointer to it. A closure can't capture an owner: capture a pointer to it instead.

Borrowing a callable: *closure(params) result. A function that only calls what it is given, while it runs, takes a borrowed closure, as it takes a *T rather than a ^T. It accepts a closure, &c, a function, &f, or a lambda written at the call. That lambda's captures go in the caller's frame, so nothing is allocated, and the call borrows it:

lora 
fn each(xs: []int, f: *closure(x: int) void) void = {
	for (let x .. xs) f(x);
}

export fn main() void = {
	let total = 0;
	let p = &total;
	each([1, 2, 3], fn(x: int) void = { *p += x; }); // no allocation
	assert(total == 6);
}

A borrowed closure can't outlive what it borrows: a function that keeps one is refused a lambda made for the call, and a lambda can be a *closure only as an argument, where the call is all it has to outlive.

lora 
fn counter(start: int) closure() int = {
	let n = start;
	return fn() int = {
		n += 1;
		return n;
	}
}

export fn main() void = {
	let next = counter(5);
	defer free(next);
	next();
	assert(next() == 7);

	let k = 1;
	let get = fn() int = k;
	defer free(get);
	k = 100;
	assert(get() == 1);       // captured by copy, at creation
}

To share a variable, capture a pointer to it:

lora 
let n = 0;
let p = &n;
let bump = fn() void = { *p += 1; }
defer free(bump);
bump();
bump();
assert(n == 2);

Ownership. A closure bound to a name is the binding's to free. A capturing lambda written directly as a call argument is a temporary, freed when the call returns, so a function taking a closure only borrows it. A function that keeps a closure (stores it, or runs it later) makes its own copy with @clone(c). coro::detach and thread::spawn do this, so coro::detach(fn() void = { ... }) leaks nothing.

lora 
fn twice(f: closure(x: int) int, x: int) int = f(f(x));

export fn main() void = {
	let k = 10;
	assert(twice(fn(x: int) int = x + k, 1) == 21);   // temporary, freed after the call
	assert(twice(fn(x: int) int = x * 2, 1) == 4);    // no captures, no allocation
}

What closures cannot do:

lora 
let n = 1;
let f: *fn() int = fn() int = n; // error: This lambda captures variables, so it is a closure
lora 
let f = fn(n: int) int = if (n == 0) 0 else f(n - 1); // error: `f` is an unknown object
  • A capturing lambda cannot become a *fn, which has no room for the environment, so it cannot be passed to C.
  • A lambda cannot refer to itself; recursion needs a named function.
  • @clone copies closures only.
  • Inside a generic function, lambdas can use its type parameters. A lambda can use locals of any enclosing function; each lambda in between captures the variable in turn.

9. Control flow

if, for, match and blocks are expressions with values.

if

lora 
let n = 7;
let kind = if (n % 2 == 0) "even" else if (n < 0) "negative" else "odd";
assert(kind == "odd");
if (n > 5) {
	n = 5;
}
assert(n == 5);

Without else, if has type (T | void):

lora 
let x: int = if (true) 1; // error: Initializer of type (void | int) is not assignable to binding type int

if let checks a tagged union or nullable pointer and binds the value. The binding must name its type:

lora 
fn find(xs: []int, v: int) (usize | void) = {
	for (let i = 0z; i < len(xs); i += 1) if (xs[i] == v) return i;
	return void;
}

export fn main() void = {
	let xs = [4, 5, 6];
	if (let i: usize = find(xs, 5)) {
		assert(i == 1);
	} else {
		abort("not found");
	}
	let x = 3;
	let p: nullable *int = &x;
	if (let q: *int = p) assert(*q == 3);
}
lora 
fn f() (int | void) = 3;
export fn main() void = {
	if (let i = f()) assert(i == 3); // error: if (let x
}

for

lora 
type counter = struct { i: int, n: int }

fn next(c: *counter) (int | done) = {
	if (c.i >= c.n) return done;
	c.i += 1;
	return c.i;
}

export fn main() void = {
	let total = 0;
	for (let i = 0; i < 10; i += 1) total += i;          // C-style
	for (let i = 0, j = 10; i < j; i += 1) total += 1;   // several bindings
	for (total < 100) total *= 2;                         // while
	let xs = [1, 2, 3];
	for (let x .. xs) total += x;                         // values
	for (let p &.. xs) *p *= 10;                          // pointers to elements
	let c = counter { i = 0, n = 3 }
	for (let v => next(&c)) total += v;                   // iterator: (T | done)
	assert(xs[2] == 30);
	for (true) break;                                     // forever
}

A for can have an else, which runs when the loop ends without break, and break value gives the loop a value:

lora 
let xs = [3, 8, 5];
let at = for (let i = 0z; i < len(xs); i += 1) {
	if (xs[i] == 8) break i;
} else len(xs);
assert(at == 1);

Labels name a loop for break and continue:

lora 
let n = 0;
for :outer (let i = 0; i < 3; i += 1) {
	for (let j = 0; j < 3; j += 1) {
		if (j == 1) continue :outer;
		n += 1;
	}
}
assert(n == 3);

What for cannot do:

lora 
for (let r .. "abc") void; // error: A for-each loop goes over an array or a slice here
lora 
for (let i .. 0..10) void; // error: syntax error
lora 
let xs = [1, 2];
for (let (i, x) .. xs) void; // error: Only a tuple can be unpacked, as in let (a, b) = t
  • for .. walks arrays and slices only. Walk a string's characters with strings::next, a map with map::iter, a range with a C-style loop.
  • There is no index binding in for ..; use a C-style loop when you need the index.
  • There is no while, do or loop keyword: for (cond) and for (true) cover them.

Blocks, yield and defer

A block is an expression. yield gives the innermost block its value, or a labeled block with yield :label, value:

lora 
let v = :outer {
	let x = 4;
	if (x > 3) yield :outer, x * 2;
	yield 0;
}
assert(v == 8);

defer expr runs expr when the enclosing block exits, however it exits, in reverse order. A return value is computed before the deferred expressions run:

lora 
fn f() int = {
	let x = 1;
	defer x = 5;
	return x;          // returns 1
}

export fn main() void = {
	let order: [2]int = [0...];
	let n = 0z;
	{
		defer { order[n] = 1; n += 1; }
		defer { order[n] = 2; n += 1; }
	}
	assert(order[0] == 2 && order[1] == 1 && f() == 1);
}
lora 
fn f() int = { defer return 1; return 2; } // error: Cannot return inside a defer
export fn main() void = void;

A deferred free of an owner is that owner's drop, whether the defer holds it alone or in a block among other statements: the owner is freed once, when the defer runs, and may be used until then.

lora 
export fn main() void = {
	let a: ^[]u8 = alloc([0...], 4)!;
	let b: ^[]u8 = alloc([0...], 4)!;
	defer {
		a[0] = 0;
		free(a);
		free(b);
	}
	a[0] = 1;
	b[0] = 2;
	assert(a[0] + b[0] == 3);
}

A defer belongs to the block it is written in, and runs when that block ends. So unsafe { defer free(p) } frees p at once, as its block is the unsafe { ... }, which is an error (L0106); and a use of what a defer in an inner block freed, after that block, is a use after free. Write the unsafe inside the defer, which then runs when the block around it ends:

lora 
export fn main() void = {
	let p = unsafe { release(alloc(10)!) };
	defer unsafe { free(p) }    // runs when main's block ends
	assert(*p == 10);
}

10. Errors

Errors are ordinary values. A type declared with ! is an error type, and a function that can fail returns a tagged union of its result and its errors. There are no exceptions. Lora's rule is that a failure always says what went wrong and why: errors describe themselves, a dropped error is warned about, and a failing program prints the error, what it was doing, and where the error came from.

lora 
use strconv;

type not_found = !void "no such record";
type parse_error = !struct { line: int } "cannot parse line {line}";

fn lookup(id: int) (str | not_found) = if (id == 1) "one" else not_found;

fn parse(s: str) (int | parse_error) = {
	if (s == "") return parse_error { line = 3 }
	return 1;
}

fn both(id: int) (int | not_found | parse_error) = {
	let name = lookup(id)?;       // ? returns the error to our caller
	return parse(name)?;
}

export fn main() void = {
	assert(lookup(1)! == "one");  // ! aborts if it is an error
	assert(both(2) is not_found);
	match (parse("")) {
		let e: parse_error => assert(e.line == 3),
		int => abort(),
	}
	let n = strconv::parse_int("42")!;
	assert(n == 42);
}

Errors that describe themselves

An error type may end with its message: a template whose {placeholders} are fields of the error, checked when compiling, or the name of a function fn(e: *const T, buf: []u8) str that describes a value. Printing an error with {}, a failing x! and a main that returns it all use the message; {:?} still shows the fields. Your own errors work exactly like the library's:

lora 
type quota = !struct { user: str, limit: usize }
"user {user} is over the limit of {limit}";

export fn main() void = {
	let e = quota { user = "ann", limit = 5 }
	let text = fmt::format("{} / {:?}", e, e)!;
	defer free(text);
	assert(text == "user ann is over the limit of 5 / quota { user = \"ann\", limit = 5 }");
}

Each library module has its own error, named <module>::error: io::error, fs::error, net::error, os::error. It says what was being done and holds the system's error number, rt::errno, which tells causes apart: cannot listen on 127.0.0.1:8080: Address already in use (EADDRINUSE, errno 48), and e.errno == rt::EADDRINUSE. Errors of different modules join in one union, (void | nomem | io::error | net::error), so each can still be matched; nothing is wrapped or lost.

A name for a union of errors only, as a library gives its errors, stands for those errors wherever it is used in a union: (T | json::error) is T or any of json's errors, each matched and passed on with ? by itself.

lora 
type too_big = !void "too big";
type too_small = !void "too small";
type bad_size = (too_big | too_small);

fn sized(n: int) (int | bad_size) =
	if (n > 9) too_big else if (n < 1) too_small else n;

fn doubled(n: int) (int | bad_size) = sized(n)? * 2;

export fn main() void = {
	assert(doubled(2)! == 4);
	match (doubled(0)) {
		int => abort(),
		too_big => abort(),
		too_small => void,
	}
}

Inferred errors: (T | !)

! in a function's result stands for the errors its body can return: the compiler gathers what its ?s and returns pass on.

lora 
use strconv;

type config = struct { port: int }
type bad_port = !struct { port: int } "port {port} is out of range";

fn load(text: str) (config | !) = {
	let port = strconv::parse_int(text)?; // strconv::invalid_number
	if (port < 1 || port > 65535) return bad_port { port = port }
	return config { port = port }
}
// load returns (config | strconv::invalid_number | bad_port)

export fn main() (void | !) = {
	let c = load("8080")?;
	fmt::println($"port {c.port}")?; // io::error, with no need to name it
}

Callers see the whole type and match each error as usual. Exported functions (other than main) write their errors out, since other modules rely on them; so do lambdas, and functions that use themselves, whose errors would depend on what they are:

lora 
use strconv;

export fn port(s: str) (int | !) = strconv::parse_int(s)?; // error: `port` is exported, so its errors must be written out

export fn main() void = void;

Handling errors

FormDoes
x?returns x's error from this function; otherwise x's value
x ? "note", x ? $"note {v}"the same, with a note for the error trace
x!aborts with the error, its notes and its trace; otherwise the value
x or yy when x is an error
x or |e| yy, with the error bound as e; y may return, break, continue or abort
matchnames each error and decides
lora 
use strconv;
use rt;

fn port(s: str) (int | strconv::invalid_number) =
	strconv::parse_int(s) ? $"reading the port {s}";

export fn main() void = {
	let a = strconv::parse_int("x") or 8080;           // a fallback
	let b = port("90") or |e| {
		fmt::eprintfn("bad port: {}", e)!;
		yield 8080;
	}
	for (let s .. ["1", "x", "3"]) {
		let n = strconv::parse_int(s) or continue;     // skip what fails
	}
	assert(a == 8080 && b == 90);
}

The function's result type must include what ? returns:

lora 
type err = !void;
fn f() (int | err) = 1;
export fn main() void = {
	let x = f()?; // error: Error type err is not assignable to function result type void
}
lora 
fn f() (int | str) = 1;
fn g() (void | str) = {
	let x = f()?; // error: No error can occur here, so there is nothing to propagate
}
export fn main() void = void;

?, ! and or look only at error types. A (T | void) optional is not an error; use ?? for it.

Traces, and main returning errors

Returning an error starts an error trace, kept per thread; each ? and each return of a caught error adds where it passed, with its note. main may return (void | errors...): when it returns an error, the program prints it, the notes (outermost first) and the trace, and exits with status 1. A failing x! prints the same.

lora 
// aborts: error: cannot parse "127.0.0.x:8080" as an IP address and port: a character that cannot be there, at byte 8
use net;
use netip;

export fn main() (void | nomem | net::error | netip::invalid) = {
	let l = net::listen_at("127.0.0.x:8080") ? "starting the server";
}

With a valid address whose port is taken, it says:

text 
error: cannot listen on 127.0.0.1:8080: Address already in use (EADDRINUSE, errno 48)
  while starting the server
  trace:
    net::listen  lib/net.lora:760:23  error made here
    main         app.lora:5:31
exit status 1
lora 
// aborts: error occurred: cannot parse line 3
type parse_error = !struct { line: int } "cannot parse line {line}";

fn parse(s: str) (int | parse_error) = parse_error { line = 3 }

export fn main() void = {
	let n = parse("x")!;
}

Errors are not dropped

A value that may be an error cannot be ignored (f(); is an error when f can fail), and a match whose _ arm takes errors that no other arm names is warned about, since the program would go on, or stop, without saying why:

lora 
use strconv;
use os;

export fn main() void = {
	let n = match (strconv::parse_int("x")) {
		let n: int => n,
		_ => os::exit(1), // warning: This `_ =>` arm drops or hides a strconv::invalid_number error
	}
}

Runtime checks say what failed too: index 5 is out of bounds for length 3, slice end 7 is beyond the length 3, 70000 does not match the pattern type port is 1..65536.

Compiler diagnostics carry a code, error[L0003], a line of help, and lora explain L0003 for the long story; every code is listed in docs/errors.md.

11. match and patterns

match takes a value and a block of arms, pattern [if guard] => expr,. Arms are tried in order and the first match wins. There is no switch.

lora 
use fmt;

fn classify(n: int) str = match n {
	0 => "zero",
	1..=9 => "digit",
	m @ 10..=99 if m % 2 == 0 => "even, two digits",
	-1 | -2 => "small negative",
	_ => "other",
}

export fn main() void = {
	assert(classify(0) == "zero" && classify(42) == "even, two digits");
	assert(classify(-2) == "small negative" && classify(43) == "other");
	match classify(5) {
		"digit" => fmt::println("a digit")!,
		_ => void,
	}
}

An arm's expression can be a block, an assignment, break, return or a call. Arms may have different types; the match's type is then a tagged union of them.

Patterns

PatternSyntaxMatches
Wildcard_anything
Literal42 "text" 'x' true nullan equal value
Constantcolor::green, LIMITan equal value
Rangea..b, a..=b (also a...b)integers and runes; .. excludes b
Bindingxanything, binding it
Referenceref xanything, binding *T to the matched value, which can be changed through it
Namedname @ patternwhat pattern matches, binding the whole value
Orp1 | p2either
Tuple(p1, p2)a tuple whose elements match
StructName { f: pat, shorthand, .. }a struct of that type; .. ignores the other fields
Array[p1, p2], [p1, ..], []arrays and slices; .. matches any tail
Typelet x: T, T, nulla tagged union member or nullable pointer, binding the value
lora 
type color = enum { red, green, blue }
type point = struct { x: int, y: int }
type line = struct { a: point, b: point }

fn first(xs: []int) int = match xs {
	[] => -1,
	[a, ..] => a,
}

export fn main() void = {
	// tuples
	let pair: (int, str) = (9, "nine");
	let r = match pair {
		(0, _) => "zero",
		(n, _) if n > 10 => "big",
		(_, name) => name,
	}
	assert(r == "nine");

	// structs, nested, with ranges and constants inside
	let l = line { a = point { x = 0, y = 1 }, b = point { x = 2, y = 3 } }
	let v = match l {
		line { a: point { x: 0, y }, b: point { x: 1..=5, .. } } => y,
		_ => -1,
	}
	assert(v == 1);

	// arrays and slices
	assert(first([7, 8]) == 7 && first([]) == -1);

	// ref: change the matched value in place
	let p = point { x = 1, y = 2 }
	match p {
		point { x: ref rx, .. } => *rx = 99,
	}
	assert(p.x == 99);

	// tagged unions and nullable pointers, by type
	let t: (int | str) = "hi";
	let len_or_value = match t {
		let i: int => i,
		let s: str => @int(len(s)),
	}
	assert(len_or_value == 2);
	let ptr: nullable *point = &p;
	match ptr {
		null => abort(),
		let q: *point => assert(q.x == 99),
	}
}

Exhaustiveness

A match on a tagged union, a nullable pointer or an enum must cover every case. A match on other values needs a _ arm:

lora 
type color = enum { red, green }
fn name(c: color) str = match c { // error: This match doesn't cover every possible value
	color::red => "red",
}
export fn main() void = void;
lora 
fn sign(n: int) int = match n { // error: This match doesn't cover every possible value
	0 => 0,
}
export fn main() void = void;

Limits

  • Or-patterns work at any depth, and name @ pattern binds the whole value wherever it appears, around any pattern:
lora 
type point = struct { x: int, y: int }

fn kind(p: (point, int)) int = match p {
	(point { x: 0 | 10, y }, _) => y,
	(whole @ point { x: 1, .. }, k) => whole.y + k,
	(point { x: n @ 2..=5, .. }, _) => n,
	_ => -1,
}

export fn main() void = {
	assert(kind((point { x = 10, y = 3 }, 0)) == 3);
	assert(kind((point { x = 1, y = 4 }, 2)) == 6);
	assert(kind((point { x = 4, y = 0 }, 0)) == 4);
}
  • The alternatives of an or-pattern cannot bind names, since each would bind different things:
lora 
fn f(p: (int, int)) int = match p {
	(a | 2, _) => 1, // error: The alternatives of an or-pattern (a | b) cannot bind names
	_ => 0,
}
export fn main() void = void;
  • Type patterns (let x: T) apply only at the top of a match on a tagged union:
lora 
let t: ((int | str), int) = (1, 2);
match t {
	(let a: int, _) => void, // error: Type patterns cannot be used inside structural patterns
	_ => void,
}
  • .. in array and struct patterns must come last; [1, .., 3] is a syntax error.
  • An empty range such as 5..2 matches nothing.
  • break :label cannot be an arm's whole expression; put it in a block: 5 => { break :outer; },.
  • Bindings are immutable; use ref x to change the matched value.

12. Memory

Locals live on the stack and are freed when their block ends. Heap memory comes from alloc, which gives an owner, ^T: a pointer that owns what it points to and frees it when it goes out of scope (see Ownership). There is no garbage collector, and no counting: an owner is as small and fast as a raw pointer. Allocation can fail, so alloc, append and insert return nomem as an error to handle with !, ? or match. An append or insert that fails leaves the slice as it was, and drops what it was given.

lora 
type node = struct { value: int, next: nullable ^node }

export fn main() void = {
	let p = alloc(42)!;                      // ^int, freed at the end of main
	let n = alloc(node { value = 1, next = null })!;
	let xs = alloc([1, 2, 3])!;              // ^[3]int, a heap copy
	let zeros = alloc([0u8...], 1024)!;      // 1024 zeroed bytes, not written
	let buf: ^[]int = alloc([], 16)!;        // empty, room for 16

	append(buf, 1)!;
	append(buf, [2, 3, 4]...)!;              // several
	insert(buf[0], 0)!;                      // at an index
	delete(buf[1]);                          // one element
	delete(buf[0..2]);                       // a range
	assert(len(buf) == 2 && buf[0] == 3);

	match (alloc(5)) {
		let q: ^int => free(q),                 // freed now, not later
		nomem => abort("out of memory"),
	}
}

A fill of zeroes, alloc([0...], n) with any value that is all zero bytes (0, false, 0.0, a struct of them), takes memory the system gives already zeroed, so a large buffer costs only the pages that are used. Any other fill, -0.0 among them, is written into every element.

Ownership

^T owns a T on the heap. Lora prefers unique ownership and borrowing:

  • One owner. An owner cannot be copied; it moves where ownership goes: to a ^T parameter, into a binding, a field or an array, or a return. A move must be the owner's last use: using it afterwards is an error, and so is a move inside a loop that the next turn would repeat.
  • Dropped automatically. An owner that has not moved is dropped when its scope ends, on every way out (return, ?, break, the end of the block): what it owns is dropped too, and its memory freed. free(p) drops it early. Owners that move somewhere carry a hidden flag so a path where they moved does not drop them; others cost nothing but the free.
  • Borrowed as *T. &p, or passing p where a *T (or *const T, or a view *T.{a}) is taken, lends it without moving it. A loan may not outlive its owner: it cannot be returned or stored in a global.
  • Fields. A field ^T is owned by what holds it: it is dropped with it, and replaced values are dropped when a new one is assigned. Moving out of a field is an error; lend it instead.
  • Escapes. release(p) gives up ownership and returns the raw *T, for code (or C) that frees it itself; adopt(raw) takes ownership of a raw pointer. Both need unsafe, as does growing a slice that isn't a ^[]T with append or insert. Outside unsafe, all heap memory has an owner. What is certain is checked in unsafe code too: adopt or free of memory no allocation made, a local's, a global's or a temporary's, is an error (L0105), as is adopting what an owner lends (a double free), and a raw pointer to memory an owner gave up leaks if it is given a new value before that memory is freed.
  • The library's types are owners too. map, set, pool::pool, regex::regex, json::document, expanse::region and coro::chan free themselves when they are dropped, and so move as an owner does. finish frees one earlier.
  • Nothing is lost. Unpacking, if let, delete and a failed append all drop what they hold. What could not be dropped is an error (L0607): leaving with ? after an owner was handed to a call or literal still being built, or from inside alloc; or with no name for an error that owns memory.
lora 
type node = struct { value: int, next: nullable ^node }

fn push(head: nullable ^node, v: int) (^node | nomem) =
	alloc(node { value = v, next = head });   // head moves into the node

fn sum(list: *node) int = {                  // borrows
	let total = 0;
	let p: nullable *node = list;
	for (true) {
		match (p) {
			null => break,
			let n: *node => {
				total += n.value;
				p = n.next;
			},
		}
	}
	return total;
}

export fn main() (void | nomem) = {
	let list = push(null, 1)?;
	list = push(list, 2)?;     // list moves into push, then owns the new head
	assert(sum(&list) == 3);   // &list lends it
}                             // the whole list is freed here
lora 
type node = struct { value: int }

fn keep(n: ^node) void = void;

export fn main() void = {
	let p = alloc(node { value = 1 })!;
	keep(p);
	let v = p.value; // error: `p` is used after it moved so it can't be used here
}
lora 
type node = struct { value: int }

fn keep(n: ^node) void = void;

export fn main() void = {
	let p = alloc(node { value = 1 })!;
	for (let i = 0; i < 3; i += 1) {
		keep(p); // error: `p` moves on every turn of the loop (line 8), but it is owned only once, so the second turn has nothing to move
	}
}
lora 
let shown: nullable *int = null;

export fn main() void = {
	let p = alloc(1)!;
	shown = &p; // error: This lends `p` where the loan outlives it
}
lora 
type node = struct { value: int }

fn show(n: *node) void = void;

export fn main() void = {
	show(alloc(node { value = 1 })!);       // lent to show, freed after the call
	let raw: *node = alloc(node { value = 1 })!; // error: This owned value is not kept by anything
}

Dropping goes through a list of what is left to drop rather than recursion, so dropping a long chain cannot overflow the stack.

Views

str, []T and *T are views: they point into memory something else owns. A view is two or three words, and making one, slicing it or passing it costs no allocation. ^str and ^[]T are the owners. The compiler tracks what each view points into, so that a view can't dangle, and nothing needs to be written for this:

  • A view can't outlive what it views. It can't be used after its source is freed, moved or out of scope (L0608).
  • A view can't leave. It can't be returned from the function its source is local to, or stored where it outlives it: a global, a returned struct, or anything a call keeps.
  • A source can't change under a view. After an append, insert, delete or assignment that may move its memory, or a call that may, views taken earlier can't be used (L0609). Taking the view again is fine.
lora 
use strings;

fn word(s: str) str = match (strings::cut(s, ' ')) { // a view of s: the caller's
	let c: (str, str) => c.0,
	void => s,
}

export fn main() void = {
	let line = strings::clone("hello world")!;
	let w = word(line);                      // views line
	assert(w == "hello");
	let kept = strings::clone(w)!;           // lives on its own
	free(line);
	assert(kept == "hello");
}
lora 
use strings;

fn word(s: str) str = s[..1];

export fn main() void = {
	let line = strings::clone("hello")!;
	let w = word(line);
	free(line);
	assert(w == "h"); // error: `w` views `line`, which was freed on line 8
}
lora 
export fn main() void = {
	let b: ^[]u8 = alloc([1u8, 2], 2)!;
	let head = b[..1];
	append(b, 3)!;
	assert(head[0] == 1); // error: `head` views `b`, which grew on line 4
}

Growing a list reached through a pointer moves that list. What the list holds views of doesn't move: views of those stay good, and views of the list itself don't:

lora 
type keeper = struct { vals: ^[]str }

fn keep_all(k: *keeper, args: []const str) (^[]str | nomem) = {
	let rest: ^[]str = [];
	for (let a .. args) {
		append(rest, a)?;     // views of args
		append(k.vals, a)?;   // moves k.vals, not args
	}
	return rest;
}

export fn main() void = {
	let k = keeper { vals = [] };
	let rest = keep_all(&k, ["a", "b"])!;
	assert(len(rest) == 2);
}

A pointer that was made to point elsewhere, or that was stored and then followed, still moves what it points to:

lora 
type set = struct { vals: ^[]int }

fn f(s: *set, t: *set) (void | nomem) = {
	append(t.vals, 1)?;
	let v = t.vals[..];
	s = t;
	append(s.vals, 2)?;
	assert(v[0] == 1); // error: `v` views `t`, which grew on line 7
}

export fn main() void = void;
lora 
type set = struct { vals: ^[]int }
type outer = struct { in: *set }

fn g(o: *outer, other: *set) (void | nomem) = {
	append(other.vals, 1)?;
	let v = other.vals[..];
	o.in = other;
	append(o.in.vals, 2)?;
	assert(v[0] == 1); // error: `v` views `other`, which grew on line 8
}

export fn main() void = void;
lora 
type keeper = struct { vals: ^[]str }

fn grow(k: *keeper) (void | nomem) = {
	append(k.vals, "a")?;
	let v = k.vals[..];
	append(k.vals, "b")?;
	assert(v[0] == "a"); // error: `v` views `k`, which grew on line 6
}

export fn main() void = void;

Where a function's result comes from is worked out from its body, across modules.
