A call the compiler can't see into, of a closure, a function pointer or an interface method, is taken to view all its arguments and to change what they point to, though not what is stored behind those. A value with no pointers, slices or strings anywhere in it, as a socket of numbers and addresses, is the exception: changing it only changes its bytes, so views of it stay good. When it isn't sure, it refuses. What unsafe { ... } does is its author's to get right: free of what no owner holds needs it too, as it may be a view.

Several owners: rc and arc

When data genuinely needs several owners (a graph, a cache), the library's rc[T] counts them, and drops the value with the last; rc::weak[T] points at it without keeping it alive; arc[T] is the same across threads. Sharing is always explicit, rc::share(&r), never a copy.

A value can't own itself. Values in a cycle of owners keep each other's counts above zero, and are never freed. So rc::new and arc::new refuse a type that could form one: nothing in it, at any depth, may lead back to it through rc or arc. No such type means no such value, whatever the program does. A link back is an rc::weak, and a graph has one owner of all its nodes, with weak links between them:

lora 
use rc;

type node = struct { value: int, next: (rc::weak[node] | void) }

export fn main() void = {
	let nodes: ^[]rc::rc[node] = [];
	append(nodes, rc::new(node { value = 1, next = void })!)!;
	append(nodes, rc::new(node { value = 2, next = void })!)!;
	rc::get(&nodes[0]).next = rc::downgrade(&nodes[1]);
	rc::get(&nodes[1]).next = rc::downgrade(&nodes[0]);   // a cycle of weak links
}
text 
type node = struct { next: (rc::rc[node] | void) };

let n = rc::new(node { next = void })!; // error: This value could own itself through rc
lora 
use rc;

type config = struct { port: int }

export fn main() void = {
	let a = rc::new(config { port = 80 })!;
	let b = rc::share(&a);                 // two owners
	assert(rc::count(&a) == 2 && rc::get(&b).port == 80);
}                                         // the last one drops the config

Cleaning up: impl drop

A type can say what dropping a value of it does first, by implementing drop (export impl drop for T lets other modules' owners run it too). A value of such a type is an owner too, even on the stack: it moves rather than copies, and its drop runs when its owner ends, so files, sockets and locks clean themselves up (RAII). net::listener, net::conn and fs::file close themselves this way.

lora 
let open_files = 0;

type file = struct { fd: int }

impl drop for file {
	fn drop(f: *file) void = { open_files -= 1; }
}

fn open(fd: int) file = {
	open_files += 1;
	return file { fd = fd }
}

export fn main() void = {
	{
		let a = open(3);
		let b = open(4);
		assert(open_files == 2);
	}                          // b, then a, are dropped: closed
	assert(open_files == 0);
}

static append and static insert add to a slice of a fixed array without allocating, aborting if it is full:

lora 
let storage: [8]int = [0...];
let s = storage[..0];
static append(s, 1)!;
static append(s, 2)!;
assert(len(s) == 2 && storage[1] == 2);

Ignoring a possible allocation failure is an error:

lora 
let s: ^[]int = [];
append(s, 1); // error: Cannot ignore an error here

Conventions:

  • Whoever allocates frees, usually with defer free(x) right after the allocation.
  • Library functions that return new memory say so (strings::concat, fmt::format, strings::split, …); the caller frees the result.
  • Slices returned by slicing (a[1..]) share memory: never free those.

Finding leaks

Memory that is never freed is found two ways.

Memory an owner holds (^T, ^str, ^[]T, a closure) frees itself, so it cannot leak. Raw memory only exists through unsafe: what an owner gave up with release, memory from C, and plain slices grown with append. These checks are for that memory.

As you compile, the compiler follows each local that holds new raw memory along every path out of its scope, and it is an error where the memory is certain to be unfreed: at a return (a failed ? included), a break or continue leaving its loop, the end of its block, or an assignment that overwrites the only pointer to it. The editor shows these errors as you type, with a quick fix that adds defer free(x);.

lora 
use fmt;
use strings;

type parse_error = !void;

fn check(s: str) (void | parse_error) = if (s == "") parse_error else void;

fn greet(name: str) void = {
	let s = unsafe { release(strings::concat("hello, ", name)!) } // error: `s` holds the memory allocated on line 9, and nothing frees it: it leaks when its block ends
	fmt::println(s)!;
}

fn first_word(text: str) (str | parse_error) = {
	let copy = unsafe { release(strings::clone(text)!) }
	check(text)?; // error: `copy` still holds the memory allocated on line 14 when the function returns here, and nothing frees it: it leaks
	return copy;
}

fn shout(s: str) str = {
	let out = unsafe { release(strings::clone(s)!) }
	out = unsafe { release(strings::concat(out, "!")!) } // error: `out` is given a new value here, but it is the only pointer to the memory allocated on line 20, which is never freed: it leaks
	return out;
}

export fn main() void = {
	greet("lora");
	let w = first_word("hi")!;
	defer unsafe { free(w) }
	let x = shout("hey");
	defer unsafe { free(x) }
}

A local holds new raw memory when it is bound to release(...) of an owner, to a library call returning raw memory ((str | nomem), ([]T | nomem) or (*T | nomem)), or to an empty slice that is later appended to. The error goes away once the memory is freed, deferred, returned, stored (in a struct, array, slice or global), captured by a closure, has its address taken, or is passed to one of your own functions, which may keep it. These are not reported, to keep false alarms rare:

  • memory freed on some paths but not others;
  • paths taken only when memory runs out (a ? on nomem);
  • memory from your own functions, which may hand out memory they keep (an arena, say): the run-time check covers those.

Raw memory is also reported when it goes nowhere it could be freed from: a statement whose value is dropped, an operand of a comparison, a condition, len, or an argument to a call that only borrows it. (An owned result used this way is simply freed once the call or comparison is done.)

lora 
use strings;

export fn main() void = {
	assert(unsafe { release(strings::concat("a", "b")!) } == "ab"); // error: `strings::concat` returns memory the caller must free, and nothing frees it here: it leaks
	assert(strings::concat("a", "b")! == "ab");          // an owner: freed after the comparison
}

Freeing memory twice, or using it after free, is an error when it is certain on every path (a len of a freed slice is allowed, since the length is still known; a defer that frees a local counts as its free):

lora 
type node = struct { v: int }

export fn main() void = {
	let p = alloc(node { v = 1 })!;
	free(p);
	p.v = 2; // error: `p` is used here, but the memory it owned was freed on line 5: this would touch freed memory
	let q = alloc(node { v = 1 })!;
	defer free(q);
	free(q); // error: `q` is freed here, and the defer on line 8 frees it again when its block ends: freeing it twice would crash
}

As the program runs, lora run --leaks (or LORA_LEAKS=1 with any built program) records every live allocation and, at exit, reports the ones not freed by then, grouped by where they were made, as the compiler writes its errors: the place, what was never freed (the name it was given there, or the function whose memory it is), the source line, the functions that were running, and the fix. On a terminal it has the compiler's colors, under a LEAK badge:

text 
$ lora run --leaks leaky.lora

leaky.lora:13:28: leak: `buf` was never freed: the 1000 bytes allocated on line 13 were still allocated when the program ended, and nothing freed them.

13 |	let buf = unsafe { release(alloc([0u8...], 1000)!) };
   |	                           ^

  made in buffer, called from main
  = help: Free it when you are done with it, on the line after it	defer unsafe { free(buf) }

lib/strings.lora:66:9: leak: Memory from `strings::concat` was never freed: the 28 bytes in 2 allocations made on line 66 were still allocated when the program ended, and nothing freed them.

66 |	append(out, to_bytes(b)...)?;
   |	^

  made in strings::concat, called from greet <- main
  = help: Free what it returns when you are done with it	defer unsafe { free(x) }

lora: leak check: 3 allocations (1028 bytes) never freed

A use after free or double free that the run finds stops it with the same layout: what was misused, where it was made and freed, and the fix.

  • The exit status is 23 when there are leaks; LORA_LEAKS=report reports them but keeps the program's own status.
  • Every allocation not freed at exit is reported. What still points to it decides nothing, so memory a global keeps until the end counts too.
  • LORA_FAIL_ALLOC=n, with LORA_LEAKS set, makes the nth allocation fail, to test what happens when memory runs out. Try each n in turn.
  • Freed blocks are poisoned and kept in a quarantine of recent frees (up to 1024 blocks and 16 MiB) before they are given back. Freeing one again is reported as a double free, and a block whose poison changed (written after it was freed) as a use after free, with where it was allocated and freed; either stops the program. A block that grows and moves goes into the quarantine too, so a write through a pointer taken before it moved is found as well.
  • lora run --guard (LORA_LEAKS=guard) stops the program at the first touch of freed memory, a read as well as a write, and at any access past a block's end. Each block gets pages of its own, ending against a page nothing may touch, and a freed block's pages are given up and made untouchable; the report says which block it was and where it was allocated and freed. A system call and two pages per block make it slow, a check to run when a test or unsafe code is suspect, not every time.
  • Without --leaks there is no cost beyond one test per allocation.

Pointers to the stack. A pointer to a local or parameter, or to a temporary, may not leave its function: returning one (also inside a struct, a tuple, a slice of a local array or an rt::any) or storing one in a global is an error. An explicit conversion, @*T(&x), says it is meant, for a pointer that is not used after the function returns.

lora 
let last: nullable *int = null;

fn counter() *int = {
	let n = 0;
	return &n; // error: This returns a pointer to `n`, which is gone when the function returns
}

fn remember(x: int) void = {
	last = &x; // error: This stores in a global a pointer to 'x', which is gone when the function returns
}

export fn main() void = void;

What calls do with pointers

The compiler works out what each function does with the pointers it is given, its effects: which parameters it keeps after it returns (in a global, in the heap, or in what another parameter points to), which it may return, and which it frees. You don't write them; typedefs record them for other modules as @effects(...). Calls are checked against them:

lora 
let saved: nullable *int = null;

fn stash(p: *int) void = { saved = p; }

fn f() void = {
	let x = 5;
	stash(&x); // error: A pointer to `x` is kept by stash after it returns, but `x` is gone once f returns.
}

export fn main() void = f();

The error says why: stash stores 'p' in the global 'saved' (line 3). Effects also follow copies: after let q = same(p) with a same that returns what it is given, q is the memory p is, so using q after free(p) is a use after free, and freeing both is a double free.

lora 
type node = struct { v: int }

fn same(n: *node) *node = n;

export fn main() void = {
	let p = unsafe { release(alloc(node { v = 1 })!) }
	let q = same(p);
	unsafe { free(p) }
	q.v = 2; // error: `q` is used here, but the memory it points to, `p`'s, was freed on line 8: this would touch freed memory
}

Arguments of one call. A function given a view of what another of its arguments changes would see that memory move under it, if it uses the view after the change. Each function's effects record which arguments it uses after changing which others, so such a call is an error (L0609), and one that uses the view first is not:

lora 
fn grow(a: *^[]int, b: *int) void = {
	append(a, 1)!;
	*b = 5;
}

export fn main() void = {
	let xs: ^[]int = [];
	append(xs, 1)!;
	grow(&xs, &xs[0]); // error: This argument views `xs`, which `grow` may change through its argument 1
}

Arguments that can't overlap are fine: different fields of one value, f(&b.items, &b.count), and a field held in place beside what grows, next(c, &c.cur). append and insert given what is in the slice they change, append(xs, xs[..]...) or insert(xs[1], xs[3]), read it as it was before the slice grew or shifted.

Only owners move memory. A call that can only reach views, a *T or []T to values that own nothing, may write through them but can't free, replace or grow what they point to: that takes an owner. So views of that memory stay good across calls the compiler can't see into (a closure, a function value, an interface method), and only owners the call can reach go stale. A closure that captured a pointer reaching an owner, let p = &xs, moves what that owner holds when called, and so does a function it is given to; one that only reads what it captured moves nothing.

lora 
type cursor = struct { b: []u8, i: usize }

export fn main() void = {
	let buf: ^[]u8 = [];
	append(buf, 1)!;
	let c = cursor { b = buf[..], i = 0 }
	let step = fn(c: *cursor) void = { c.i += 1; };
	let v = c.b;
	step(&c);       // writes c, can't move buf
	assert(v[0] == 1 && c.i == 1);
}
lora 
export fn main() void = {
	let xs: ^[]int = [];
	append(xs, 1)!;
	let p = &xs;
	let g = fn() void = { let q = p; append(q, 2)!; };
	let v = &xs[0];
	g();
	*v = 5; // error: `v` views `xs`, which was changed by the closure called on line 7, so its memory may have moved.
}

Limits. Use after free is found when it is certain at compile time, or, under --leaks, when freed memory is written while it is in the quarantine; reads of freed memory see the poison but are not reported, except under LORA_LEAKS=guard, which stops at any touch of it. Calls through function pointers, closures and interface values are assumed not to keep their arguments, as are C functions; so a function that keeps one can't be made a function value: &keep, for a keep that stores its argument in a global, is an error (L0608), and nor can a type be made an interface value if one of its methods keeps what it is given. Keeping an argument in what another argument points to counts as keeping it, for a function value:

lora 
type state = struct { last: str }

fn keep(s: *state, v: str) void = { s.last = v; };

export fn main() void = {
	let f = &keep; // error: keep keeps `v` after it returns, so it can't be made a function value
}

Memory reached by following a pointer read from memory is of unknown lifetime. Closures given to @all, @first and @scope share pointers with the code that starts them, which always waits for them; thread::spawn and coro::detach take none: what they change is checked for data races instead (concurrency).

13. Generics

Functions and types take type parameters in brackets. Generics are monomorphized: each set of type arguments gets its own compiled code, so there is no boxing and no runtime cost.

lora 
fn max[T: ordered](a: T, b: T) T = if (a > b) a else b;

type pair[A, B] = struct { a: A, b: B }
type node[T] = struct { value: T, next: nullable *node[T] }
type result[T] = (T | str);

fn first[A, B](p: pair[A, B]) A = p.a;
fn zero[T: numeric]() T = @T(0);

export fn main() void = {
	assert(max(3, 7) == 7);                    // T = int, inferred
	assert(max::[u8](200, 100) == 200);        // explicit
	let wide: u64 = max(1, 2);                 // T = u64, from the expected type
	let x: u8 = zero();                        // inferred from the result alone
	let p = pair { a = 1, b = "x" }           // pair[int, str]
	let q: pair[str, bool] = pair { a = "y", b = true }
	assert(first(p) == 1 && q.b && wide == 2 && x == 0);
	let n = node { value = 2, next = null }
	let r: result[int] = 5;
	assert(n.value == 2 && r is int);
	let f = &max::[f64];                       // a generic function as a value
	let g: *fn(a: int, b: int) int = &max;     // or from the target type
	assert(f(1.0, 2.0) == 2.0 && g(5, 4) == 5);
}

Type arguments in part. f::[A, B] may give fewer type arguments than f has: those given are the first ones, and the call's arguments infer the rest. It is for a type the arguments can't say, such as what a function makes or gives back, while the rest follows from what is passed:

lora 
fn convert[T, U](u: U) T = @T(u);
fn total[T](xs: []i64, scale: T) i64 = {
	let t = 0i64;
	for (let x .. xs) t += x;
	return t * @i64(scale);
}

export fn main() void = {
	assert(convert::[i64](3i32) == 3);   // T given, U from 3i32
	assert(total([1, 2, 3], 2) == 12);    // [1, 2, 3] is a []i64, as the parameter says
}

A parameter whose type names none of the type parameters checks its argument as any call does, so [1, 2, 3], [] and ["a", 1i64] take its type. Another name for an instance, type ints = box[int], is that instance, not a type of its own.

lora 
fn convert[T, U](u: U) T = @T(u);
export fn main() void = {
	convert::[i64, i32, u8](3i32); // error: convert expects 2 type arguments, got 3.
}
lora 
fn pick[A, B, C](b: B) A = @A(b);
export fn main() void = {
	pick::[i64](3i32); // error: Cannot infer type parameter `C` of pick from the arguments
}

Constraints state what a type parameter must support, and are checked at the call. Built in: ordered (numbers, and runes by code point), numeric, integer, signed, unsigned, float and equatable (types == compares). Any interface is a constraint too. Without a constraint, the body is checked for each instantiation:

lora 
fn max[T: ordered](a: T, b: T) T = if (a > b) a else b;
export fn main() void = {
	max("a", "b"); // error: str does not satisfy the constraint `ordered` on type parameter T of max
}
lora 
fn neg[T](x: T) T = -x; // error: Only numbers can be negated
export fn main() void = { neg("str"); }

Generics work across modules: exported generic functions and types are written into the module's typedef and compiled in each module that uses them (sort::sort, map::map[K, V], coro::chan[T]). Their names are their own module's, so a constraint from a module the user does not import, as flag::add_text's encoding::text_decoder, is still found and checked.

What generics cannot do:

lora 
fn make[T]() T = 0;
export fn main() void = {
	make(); // error: Cannot infer type parameter `T` of make from the arguments
}
lora 
fn max[T: ordered](a: T, b: T) T = if (a > b) a else b;
export fn main() void = {
	let f = &max; // error: Cannot use the generic function max as a value without type arguments
}
lora 
fn f[T: ordered + equatable](a: T) T = a; // error: syntax error: expected ']', found '+'
export fn main() void = void;
lora 
fn f[T = int](a: T) T = a; // error: syntax error: expected ']', found '='
export fn main() void = void;
lora 
fn first[T, N](xs: [N]T) T = xs[0];
export fn main() void = {
	let a = [1, 2];
	first(a); // error: Cannot infer type parameter `N` of first from the arguments
}
  • Type parameters are types only: no constant parameters such as an array length. Take a slice instead.
  • One constraint per parameter, and no default type arguments.
  • No specialization: one body serves every instantiation.
  • impl blocks can be generic; see Interfaces.

14. Interfaces

An interface names a set of methods. An impl provides them for a type: each method takes a pointer to the type first (the receiver), then the parameters the interface declares.

lora 
type shape = interface {
	fn area() f64;
	fn scale(k: f64) void;
}

type circle = struct { r: f64 }
type square = struct { side: f64 }

impl shape for circle {
	fn area(c: *circle) f64 = 3.0 * c.r * c.r;
	fn scale(c: *circle, k: f64) void = { c.r *= k; }
}

impl shape for square {
	fn area(s: *square) f64 = s.side * s.side;
	fn scale(s: *square, k: f64) void = { s.side *= k; }
}

fn total[T: shape](xs: []T) f64 = {          // an interface as a constraint
	let t = 0.0;
	for (let x &.. xs) t += x.area();
	return t;
}

export fn main() void = {
	let c = circle { r = 1.0 }
	c.scale(2.0);                              // static dispatch
	assert(c.area() == 12.0);

	let s = square { side = 2.0 }
	let shapes: [_]shape = [&c, &s];           // interface values: dynamic dispatch
	let sum = 0.0;
	for (let sh .. shapes) sum += sh.area();
	assert(sum == 16.0);

	let squares = [square { side = 1.0 }, square { side = 3.0 }];
	assert(total(squares[..]) == 10.0);
}
  • x.name(args) calls a method when x has no field name. On a value or pointer of a type with an impl, the call is direct. A pointer to x is passed as the receiver.
  • An interface value is two words: a pointer to the value and its type's method table. It is made from a pointer, which must outlive it; methods called through it can change the original.
  • Interfaces can be implemented for built-in types and for another module's types, and can be generic:
lora 
type named = interface { fn name() str; }
impl named for int { fn name(x: *int) str = "int"; }

type getter[T] = interface { fn get() T; }
type box = struct { v: int }
impl getter[int] for box { fn get(b: *box) int = b.v; }

export fn main() void = {
	let n = 3;
	assert(n.name() == "int");
	let b = box { v = 7 }
	let g: getter[int] = &b;
	assert(g.get() == 7);
}

A method that only reads its receiver may take it as *const T: it can then be called on a *const T too. @implements(T, I) asks, while compiling, whether T has an impl of I, so a generic function can use one where there is one:

lora 
type named = interface { fn name() str; }
type cat = struct { n: str }
impl named for cat { fn name(c: *const cat) str = c.n; }

fn label[T](v: *const T) str = {
	@if (@implements(T, named)) {
		return v.name();
	} else {
		return "?";
	}
}

export fn main() void = {
	let c = cat { n = "tom" }
	assert(label(&c) == "tom" && label(&3) == "?");
	assert(@implements(cat, named) && !@implements(int, named));
}

What interfaces cannot do:

lora 
type shape = interface { fn area() f64; }
type sq = struct { s: f64 }
impl shape for sq { fn area(q: *sq) f64 = q.s * q.s; }
export fn main() void = {
	let q = sq { s = 2.0 }
	let sh: shape = q; // error: Initializer of type sq is not assignable to binding type shape
}
lora 
type shape = interface { fn area() f64; fn name() str; }
type sq = struct { s: f64 }
impl shape for sq { fn area(q: *sq) f64 = q.s; } // error: The impl of shape for sq is missing method `name`
export fn main() void = void;
lora 
type shape = interface { fn area() f64; }
type sq = struct { s: f64 }
impl shape for sq { fn area(q: *sq) f64 = q.s; }
impl shape for sq { fn area(q: *sq) f64 = q.s; } // error: shape is already implemented for sq
export fn main() void = void;
lora 
type sq = struct { s: f64 }
fn area(q: *sq) f64 = q.s;
export fn main() void = {
	let q = sq { s = 1.0 }
	q.area(); // error: `area` is not a field of this struct
}
  • Methods exist only through impl; there are no free-standing methods.
  • A type implements an interface at most once. When a type implements two interfaces with a method of the same name, x.name() is ambiguous; call through an interface value instead.
  • export impl makes an impl visible to importers.

Generic impls

impl[T] I for box[T] { ... } implements an interface for every instance of a generic type. Each instance that needs it gets its own impl, made the first time it is used:

lora 
type getter[T] = interface { fn get() T; }
type named = interface { fn name() str; }
type box[T] = struct { v: T }
type pair[A, B] = struct { a: A, b: B }

impl[T] getter[T] for box[T] {
	fn get(b: *box[T]) T = b.v;
}

impl[A, B] named for pair[A, B] {
	fn name(p: *pair[A, B]) str = "pair";
}

export fn main() void = {
	let b = box { v = 41 }
	let s = box { v = "hi" }
	assert(b.get() == 41 && s.get() == "hi");    // getter[int] and getter[str]
	let g: getter[int] = &b;
	assert(g.get() == 41);
	let p = pair { a = 1, b = true }
	assert(p.name() == "pair");
}

Every type parameter of a generic impl must appear in the type it is for.

Embedding

An interface can include another's methods by naming it. A type that implements the larger interface implements each embedded one too, and a value of the larger one converts to any interface it embeds, at no cost: it keeps the same value, and its method table from where that interface's methods are.

The other way, a type that implements each part with an impl of its own implements the interface made of them, with no impl of that: given impls of reader and of closer, it is a read_closer too. Two impls that give the same method different bodies make no such interface.

lora 
type shape = interface { fn area() f64; }
type named_shape = interface { shape; fn name() str; }

type sq = struct { s: f64 }
impl named_shape for sq {
	fn area(q: *sq) f64 = q.s * q.s;
	fn name(q: *sq) str = "square";
}

fn area_of(s: shape) f64 = s.area();

export fn main() void = {
	let q = sq { s = 3.0 }
	let n: named_shape = &q;
	let s: shape = n;                        // shape's methods are named_shape's too
	assert(s.area() == 9.0 && area_of(&q) == 9.0 && n.name() == "square");
}
lora 
type getter = interface { fn get() int; }
type setter = interface { fn set(v: int) void; }
type both = interface { getter; setter; }

type cell = struct { v: int }
impl getter for cell { fn get(c: *cell) int = c.v; }
impl setter for cell { fn set(c: *cell, v: int) void = { c.v = v; } }

fn reset(s: setter) void = s.set(0);

export fn main() void = {
	let c = cell { v = 5 }
	let b: both = &c;          // made of the impls of its parts
	reset(b);                  // and passed as the part it embeds second
	assert(b.get() == 0);
}

Default methods

A method can have a default body, used by impls that leave it out. In the body, self is a pointer to the implementing type, so other methods called on it are that type's own:

lora 
type shape = interface {
	fn area() f64;
	fn name() str = "a shape";
	fn describe() str = self.area() > 10.0 ? "big" : "small";
}

type sq = struct { s: f64 }
type circle = struct { r: f64 }

impl shape for sq {
	fn area(q: *sq) f64 = q.s * q.s;
}

impl shape for circle {
	fn area(c: *circle) f64 = 3.0 * c.r * c.r;
	fn name(c: *circle) str = "circle";            // replaces the default
}

export fn main() void = {
	let q = sq { s = 4.0 }
	let c = circle { r = 1.0 }
	assert(q.name() == "a shape" && q.describe() == "big");
	assert(c.name() == "circle" && c.describe() == "small");
}

Defaults cross module boundaries with the interface. Generic interfaces cannot have default bodies yet.

Fields

An interface can require fields, name: T;. A type implementing it must have a field of that name and type, anywhere in its layout; through an interface value the field can be read and changed:

lora 
type named = interface {
	name: str;
	count: int;
	fn greet() str = self.name;
}

type user = struct { id: int, name: str, count: int }
type robot = struct { model: u8, count: int, name: str }

impl named for user {}
impl named for robot {
	fn greet(r: *robot) str = "beep";
}

fn bump(n: named) void = { n.count += 1; }

export fn main() void = {
	let u = user { id = 1, name = "ada", count = 0 }
	let r = robot { model = 7, count = 10, name = "r2" }
	let all: [_]named = [&u, &r];
	bump(all[0]);
	bump(all[1]);
	assert(all[0].name == "ada" && u.count == 1 && r.count == 11);
	assert(all[1].greet() == "beep");
}
lora 
type named = interface { name: str; }
type t = struct { name: int }
impl named for t {} // error: named needs t to have a field `name` of type str
export fn main() void = void;

15. Macros

macro name(params) = body; declares a macro and @name(args) expands it. Expansion happens while type checking, so the result is ordinary, fully checked code. Each use of a parameter is the caller's argument expression, so arguments can be assigned to, see the caller's names, and are evaluated where and as often as they are used:

lora 
macro swap(a, b) = {
	let tmp = a;          // the body's own names never capture the caller's
	a = b;
	b = tmp;
}
macro unless(cond, body) = if (!(cond)) body;
macro guard(cond) = if (!(cond)) return 0;      // returns from the caller

fn checked(x: int) int = {
	@guard(x > 0);
	return x;
}

export fn main() void = {
	let tmp = 1, b = 2;
	@swap(tmp, b);
	assert(tmp == 2 && b == 1);
	let ran = false;
	@unless(tmp > 5, ran = true);
	assert(ran && checked(-1) == 0 && checked(3) == 3);
}
lora 
macro twice(x) = x + x;
fn bump(p: *int) int = { *p += 1; return *p; }

export fn main() void = {
	let n = 0;
	let r = @twice(bump(&n));   // bump runs twice: 1 + 2
	assert(n == 2 && r == 3);
}

export macro makes a macro available to importers, called @module::name(...), or @name(...) after use module::{name}.

What macros cannot do:

lora 
macro twice(x) = x + x;
export fn main() void = {
	@twice(1, 2); // error: Macro '@twice' takes 1 argument, got 2
}
lora 
macro r(x) = @r(x); // error: Macro '@r' is expanded more than 64 levels deep
export fn main() void = { @r(1); }
  • A macro takes a fixed number of arguments: no variadic or optional ones.
  • Expansion nests at most 64 levels.
  • Macros are not values; they cannot be passed or stored.
  • Names in the body other than parameters resolve where the macro is used.
  • comptime, clone, typename, typeinfo and undefined are built-in macros; a module's own macros of those names take precedence.

16. Compile-time execution

@comptime(expr) runs an expression while compiling, calling ordinary functions, and puts the resulting constant in its place. Use it anywhere a constant is needed:

lora 
use strings;

type range = struct { lo: int, hi: int }

fn fib(n: int) int = if (n < 2) n else fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);

fn squares() [5]int = {
	let out: [5]int = [0...];
	for (let i = 0z; i < 5; i += 1) out[i] = @int(i * i);
	return out;
}

fn bounds() range = range { lo = 1, hi = fib(10) }

def FIB20: int = @comptime(fib(20));                 // 6765, computed once

export fn main() void = {
	let table: [@comptime(fib(6))]u8 = [0...];        // an 8-element array
	let sq = @comptime(squares());
	let r = @comptime(bounds());
	const shout = @comptime(strings::toupper("abc")!);   // other modules too
	assert(FIB20 == 6765 && len(table) == 8 && sq[4] == 16 && r.hi == 55);
	assert(shout == "ABC");
}

The interpreter runs locals and assignment, if, match (every pattern, guards, ? and !), every kind of for, yield, return, assert, calls (recursion, other modules' functions), arithmetic, comparisons and casts, over integers, floats, bools, runes, strings, arrays, structs, tuples, tagged unions and slices. Pointers into locals, elements, fields and alloced memory work, append grows slices, and globals read their initial values.

What cannot run at compile time:

lora 
@symbol("abs") fn c_abs(x: i32) i32;
def X: i32 = @comptime(unsafe { c_abs(-1) }); // error: This function has no body that can run at compile time (a C function, say)
export fn main() void = void;
lora 
fn mk() ^[2]int = alloc([1, 2])!;
export fn main() void = {
	let p = @comptime(mk()); // error: The result of @comptime can't hold pointers or slices into memory made at compile time
}
lora 
fn d() int = { defer void; return 1; } // error: defer cannot be evaluated at compile time
export fn main() void = { let p = @comptime(d()); }
  • C functions, system calls and I/O.
  • defer.
  • Results holding pointers or slices into memory made at compile time; return values (arrays, structs, strings) instead.
  • Reading memory as an unrelated type (reading a str as []u8, as strings does, works).
  • More than 10 million steps or 512 nested calls: evaluation stops with an error.

17. Reflection

@typename(T) is a type's name. @typeinfo(T) is a *rt::typeinfo, static metadata the compiler emits. To name rt::type_kind, add use rt;.

text 
type rt::typeinfo = struct {
	name: str,
	kind: rt::type_kind,     // VOID BOOL INT UINT FLOAT RUNE STR POINTER SLICE
	                         // ARRAY STRUCT UNION TAGGED TUPLE ENUM FUNCTION ...
	bytes: usize, alignment: usize,
	id: u32,                 // the same in every module
	elem: nullable *rt::typeinfo,   // of a pointer, slice or array
	length: usize,                  // of an array
	fields: []rt::field,     // struct, union and tuple fields; tagged members
}
type rt::field = struct { name: str, at: usize, typeinfo: *rt::typeinfo };
lora 
use fmt;
use rt;

type point = struct { x: int, label: str }

fn describe(ti: *rt::typeinfo) void = {
	for (let f .. ti.fields) {
		fmt::printfn($"{f.name} at {f.at}: {f.typeinfo.name}")!;
	}
}

fn kind_of[T](x: T) rt::type_kind = @typeinfo(T).kind;

export fn main() void = {
	let ti = @typeinfo(point);
	assert(ti.kind == rt::type_kind::STRUCT && len(ti.fields) == 2);
	assert(@typename(point) == "point" && ti.bytes == 32);
	describe(ti);
	assert(kind_of(1.5) == rt::type_kind::FLOAT);

	// any value, viewed with its type info
	let v: rt::any = point { x = 1, label = "a" }
	assert(v.typeinfo.kind == rt::type_kind::STRUCT);
	let p = unsafe { @*const point(v.value) } // the type info says it is one
	assert(p.x == 1);
}
  • rt::any describes a value: struct { value: nullable *const opaque, typeinfo: *rt::typeinfo }. Any value converts to it implicitly, by its address (a value with no address of its own is held in a temporary of the enclosing function), so nothing is copied; the view is valid as long as the value is. fmt prints its arguments this way.
  • A tagged union's fields are its members, in which at is where the value follows the tag, and the tag is the member's id. An enum's fields are its members, in which at is the member's value.
  • Types that refer to themselves work, since typeinfos point at each other.
  • Each module has its own copies, so compare typeinfos by id, not by address.
lora 
let x = 3;
let ti = @typeinfo(x); // error: `x` is not a type: it names something else

18. Optionals

?T is short for (T | void), a value that may be missing. a ?? b is a's value, or b when a is void; it works the same on nullable pointers (b when a is null). a is evaluated once and b only when needed, and b can leave the function:

lora 
fn find(xs: []int, v: int) ?usize = {
	for (let i = 0z; i < len(xs); i += 1) if (xs[i] == v) return i;
	return void;
}

fn index_or_fail(xs: []int, v: int) int = {
	let i = find(xs, v) ?? return -1;          // an early exit
	return @int(i);
}

export fn main() void = {
	let xs = [1, 2, 3];
	assert(find(xs, 3) ?? 99 == 2);
	assert(find(xs, 9) ?? 99 == 99);
	assert(index_or_fail(xs, 9) == -1);
	let fallback = 0;
	let p: nullable *int = null;
	assert(*(p ?? &fallback) == 0);            // nullable *T ?? *T is *T
	match find(xs, 2) {
		let i: usize => assert(i == 1),
		void => abort(),
	}
}

?? binds more loosely than arithmetic and more tightly than comparisons, and groups to the right: a ?? b ?? c.

An optional is not an error, so ? does not apply to it:

lora 
fn f() ?int = void;
fn g() ?int = {
	let x = f()?; // error: No error can occur here, so there is nothing to propagate
	return x;
}
export fn main() void = void;

19. String interpolation

$"..." holds expressions in braces and is a str. {{ and }} are literal braces. It needs no use fmt, and what it costs depends on where it is:

  • As a format string, the argument before a function's rt::any... parameter, it expands to the format string and its values: fmt::printfn($"{a} + {b}") is fmt::printfn("{} + {}", a, b). No string is made.
  • Borrowed, as another call argument (a str parameter, as in fmt::println($"...")), in len($"...") or $"...".len(), it is a temporary string, freed as soon as the call is done.
  • Kept, when it is bound, assigned, returned or stored, it is an owned string, ^str, freed when its owner ends: let s = $"..." is let s = fmt::string(...).

Running out of memory while making one aborts.

lora 
fn center() (int, int) = (3, 4);

export fn main() void = {
	let name = "lora", n = 3;
	fmt::printfn($"{name} has {n} items, {n * 2} doubled, {{literal}}")!;
	fmt::println($"center: {center().0}, {center().1}")!; // a temporary
	let width = $"center: {center().0}".size();             // also one
	assert(width == 9);
	let s = $"{n}!";                                       // kept: a ^str
	assert(s == "3!" && s.len() == 2);
}                                                         // s is freed here

A spec follows the expression after a colon, as in fmt: $"{n:x} {ratio:.2} {name:>8}" is ("{:x} {:.2} {:>8}", n, ratio, name). The last colon outside brackets begins the spec when what follows it is a spec; write {(a ? b : x)} to print a conditional whose last part looks like one.

lora 
use fmt;

export fn main() void = {
	let n = 255, pi = 3.14159;
	let s = $"{n:#x} {pi:.2} [{n:>5}] {[1, 2]:?}";
	defer free(s);
	assert(s == "0xff 3.14 [  255] [1, 2]");
}

A literal format string passed with values to a function taking rt::any... is checked when compiling: each placeholder must be well formed, and there must be a value for each.

lora 
use fmt;

export fn main() void = {
	fmt::printfn("{} and {}", 1)!; // error: This format string needs 2 values, but 1 is given
}

20. Concurrency

Lora's concurrent work runs as coroutines (coro): lightweight tasks on a pool of threads, which move between them. There is no async and no await: any function can run concurrently, and a coroutine waits inside the calls that wait (a channel, coro::sleep, a socket), letting others run. Work is started by three forms that wait for it, so it is part of the code that starts it:

FormRunsGives
@all(f(), g())each expressiona tuple of their values, or the first error
@all for (let x .. xs) f(x)the expression for each turn of the loopan owned slice of the values, in order, or the first error
@first(f(), g())each expressionthe first value to come, or the last error if all fail
@scope { ... }@go f(x) anywhere in its blockthe block's value, or the first error of a child
@each for (let x .. xs) f(x) => |r| handlethe expression for each turn of the loopnothing: handle takes each result r as its child finishes
lora 
use coro;

type gone = !void "gone";

fn profile(id: int) (str | gone) = if (id < 0) gone else "ann";
fn orders(id: int) (int | gone) = id * 10;

fn dashboard(id: int) ((str, int) | gone | coro::cancelled) = {
	// both run at once, and @all waits for both
	let (name, count) = @all(profile(id), orders(id))?;
	return (name, count);
}

export fn main() void = {
	let (name, count) = dashboard(7)!;
	assert(name == "ann" && count == 70);
	assert(dashboard(-1) is gone);
}
  • The work is the code's own. A form ends only once all of its work has, on every way out of it, so a child can use the locals and views of the code around it: nothing it uses can go away first.
  • The first failure ends it. The other children are cancelled and waited for, and the form gives that error, with a type that says which errors it can be. ?, or and match handle it as any error.
  • Cancelling is cooperative. A cancelled child's waits end at once: a receive or send is done, coro::sleep returns, and a socket read or write fails with ECANCELED. Long work asks with coro::check()? or coro::is_cancelled(). Cancelling a scope cancels the scopes its children have open. Every form can be cancelled, so each can give coro::cancelled.
  • Options, in the parentheses: within = ms cancels the work if it is not done in time, and gives coro::timed_out; max = n (for @all for) runs at most n children at once; workers = n runs the work on n threads when nothing runs coroutines yet.
lora 
use coro;

fn slow(ms: u64) int = {
	coro::sleep(ms);
	return 1;
}

export fn main() void = {
	// the first to come wins, and the other is cancelled
	assert(@first(slow(500), slow(1))! == 1);
	// too slow: cancelled, and timed out
	assert(@all(slow(1000), within = 10) is coro::timed_out);
	let ns = [1, 2, 3];
	let ones = @all(max = 2) for (let n .. ns) slow(1);
	let got = ones!;
	assert(len(got) == 3);
	free(got);
}

@scope is for children started as the code goes, as by a server for each connection. @go starts one, in the innermost @scope:

lora 
use coro;
use thread;

export fn main() void = {
	let hits = thread::atomic { ... }
	let ph = &hits;
	@scope {
		for (let i = 0; i < 10; i += 1) @go thread::add(ph, 1);
	}!;
	assert(thread::load(&hits) == 10);
}
lora 
use coro;
export fn main() void = { @go void; } // error: @go starts a child of the @scope it is in, and this is in none.

Children start running at once, in a coroutine or not: in main, outside any coroutine, the scope's children run on worker threads while its block goes on, so a loop that accepts connections and starts a child for each serves them as they come. The block's end waits for them all.

When @go f(..., x, ...) gives an owner x that is a local, x moves into the child, which drops it when f returns: a connection each child serves and closes, a buffer it fills. The code after can't use x, and a call gives one owner this way; more go together in a struct or tuple.

lora 
use coro;
use strings;

fn check(s: ^str) void = assert(s == "hi");

export fn main() void = {
	@scope {
		let s = strings::clone("hi")!;
		@go check(s);   // s is the child's now
	}!;
}

@each handles results as they come, errors included: a ? in the handler returns from the function, which cancels the children still running and waits for them, as every way out does. Results not yet taken are dropped. Run from outside any coroutine, the children all run first, and their results come in the order they finished.

lora 
use coro;

type gone = !void "gone";

fn slow(ms: u64) (u64 | gone) = {
	coro::sleep(ms);
	return if (ms == 7) gone else ms;
}

fn first_two(ms: []u64) ([2]u64 | gone | coro::cancelled) = {
	let got: [2]u64 = [0...];
	let n = 0z;
	@each for (let m .. ms) slow(m) => |r| {
		if (n < 2) got[n] = r?;
		n += 1;
	}?;
	return got;
}

export fn main() void = {
	let got = @all(first_two([30, 10, 20]))!;
	assert(got[0] == 10 && got[1] == 20);
	assert(@all(first_two([30, 7, 20])) is gone);
}

What children inherit. A child of @all, @first, @each or @scope starts with what its parent has: its cancellation and deadline, its priority, and its task-local values. A detached coroutine starts with none of these.

  • Priority. coro::priority is low, normal or high: a ready coroutine runs before those of lower priority. priority = p sets a form's children's, coro::set_priority(p) the running coroutine's, and a coroutine waiting for its children raises theirs to its own, so work it waits for is never held up behind it.
  • Task-local values. coro::bind(&key, v, fn() R = ...) binds key to v for the length of the call, for the coroutine and every child it starts there; coro::lookup(&key) gives it, or void. Each reads a copy, so a value can't point into memory or own it.
lora 
use coro;

let request: coro::local[u64] = coro::local { name = "request" }

fn current() u64 = match (coro::lookup(&request)) {
	let r: u64 => r,
	void => 0,
}

export fn main() void = {
	let (a, b) = coro::bind(&request, 42u64, fn() (u64, u64) =
		@all(current(), current())!);
	assert(a == 42 && b == 42 && current() == 0);
}

Serial values. coro::serial[T] is a value one coroutine at a time uses, as an actor's state is: coro::with(&s, fn(v: *T) R = ...) runs the closure on it, while others wait their turn as coroutines. The closure may not wait itself (the compiler checks), so a turn is short and the value can't change in the middle of one: read or change it, and wait before or after.

lora 
use coro;

fn add(t: *coro::serial[int], n: int) int =
	coro::with(t, fn(v: *int) int = {
	*v += n;
	return *v;
});

export fn main() void = {
	let total = coro::serial_new(0);
	let pt = &total;
	let sums = @all for (let n .. [1, 2, 3]) add(pt, n);
	let each = sums!;
	assert(len(each) == 3);
	free(each);
	assert(coro::with(&total, fn(v: *int) int = *v) == 6);
}

Detached coroutines. coro::detach(fn() void = ...) starts work that nothing waits for, which may outlive the code that started it, so it takes only what it owns: the compiler refuses a capture that points into memory it doesn't own. coro::detach_with(v, fn(v: T) void = ...) gives it an owned value, such as an arc share, and coro::run() runs detached coroutines until all have finished. Each gives a coro::detached, which coro::cancel(d) cancels (its waits end at once, as a cancelled child's do) and coro::running(d) asks about; it is an id, never reused, so it may be kept and copied, and cancelling one that has finished does nothing.

lora 
use coro;
fn start() void = {
	let n = 0;
	let p = &n;
	coro::detach(fn() void = { *p = 7; })!; // error: A detached coroutine may outlive `p`, which is a *int, a view of memory it doesn't own: it takes only what it owns.
}
export fn main() void = start();

A plain function, *fn, views nothing that can end, as its code lasts as long as the program: a detached coroutine may be given one, with the value it works on.

lora 
use coro;

fn count(c: *int) void = { *c += 1; };

export fn main() void = {
	let f: *fn(c: *int) void = &count;
	coro::detach_with(f, fn(f: *fn(c: *int) void) void = {
		let n = 0;
		f(&n);
		assert(n == 1);
	})!;
	coro::run();
}
  • Coroutines are cooperative: one runs until it waits. A loop that never does holds its worker thread; coro::yield_now() lets others run.
  • Code in coroutines on different workers runs in parallel: protect what they share with channels, coro::serial, thread::mutex or atomics.
  • Blocking C calls belong in coro::blocking(fn() void = ...), which moves them off the scheduler.
  • Threads (thread::spawn, thread::spawn_with) are OS threads, joined with thread::join, which take only what they own (below).

Data races

Code started on another thread, a closure given to thread::spawn, coro::detach or coro::blocking, a child of @all, @first or @scope, and every function of the module it calls, runs at the same time as the code that started it. The compiler checks that it does not change data other threads may use without synchronising:

  • it may not change a mutable global, or read one that other code changes;
  • children that run at the same time (of one @all, @first or @scope, or started in a loop, as @all for does) may not reach the same data when one of them may change it;
  • a @go child may not reach data it may change at all, as the code of its @scope runs beside it.

What a child reaches is worked out from the types of what it captures, not from what its code happens to do: a *T or []T reaches data of type T it may change, a *const T or []const T data it only reads, and a pointer inside a struct, or inside data a pointer reaches, counts too. So a function the child passes a pointer to, or a pointer it reads from memory, can't change shared data unseen. Two children reach the same data when they reach data of one type, or of a type holding the other (a *point and a *f64 may both reach a point's x), unless each points at a different local, by let p = &x given no other value, of a type holding no pointers itself: two connections, two counters. What one child captures is used by that child alone, one thing after another, so it is not compared with itself.

Shared data is fine when it is thread-safe: a thread::atomic, a thread::mutex or thread::cond, a coro::chan, coro::group or coro::serial, or a thread::shared::[T], a value guarded by a lock that threads reach one at a time with thread::with. Code between thread::lock(m) and thread::unlock(m) in the same block holds the lock, and a global marked @synchronised is guarded by its module itself (as coro's scheduler state is, by its lock). A struct type marked @synchronised is thread-safe too: its module guards it, and only its module touches its fields, as with allocator::atomic_fixed_buffer and sql::db.

An interface value can't be shared: what it points to may be of any type. Share a pointer to the thread-safe value itself, and make the interface in the child:

lora 
use allocator;
use coro;

export fn main() void = {
	let af = allocator::atomic_fixed_buffer_owned(4096)!;
	let p = &af;                                 // thread-safe: shared
	@scope {
		for (let w = 0; w < 4; w += 1) {
			@go {
				let a: allocator::allocator = p;
				let x = allocator::create(a, w)!;
				assert(*x == w);
			};
		}
	}!;
}
lora 
use thread;

let counter = 0;

export fn main() void = {
	let t = thread::spawn(fn() void = {
		counter += 1; // error: `counter` is changed by a thread while other threads may use it.
	})!;
	thread::join(t);
}

The fixes are a thread::atomic, or a shared value:

lora 
use coro;
use thread;

export fn main() void = {
	let hits = thread::new_shared(0);
	let ph = &hits;
	@scope {
		for (let i = 0; i < 4; i += 1) {
			@go thread::with(ph, fn(n: *int) void = { *n += 1; });
		}
	}!;
	thread::with(&hits, fn(n: *int) void = assert(*n == 4));
}

What a @go child points into stays put until its @scope ends, as the child may run until then: the @scope's own code can't move, free or end it before.

lora 
use coro;
use thread;

export fn main() void = {
	let names: ^[]str = [];
	append(names, "ada")!;
	let shared = thread::new_shared(names);
	let p = &shared;
	@scope { // error: A @go child of this @scope uses `shared`, which moved on line 11
		@go thread::with(p, fn(v: *^[]str) void = assert(len(v) == 1));
		let moved = shared;
	}!;
}

A thread, thread::spawn(fn() void = ...), may outlive the code that starts it, so like coro::detach it takes only what it owns: copies its lambda captures, and a value given with thread::spawn_with(v, fn(v: T) void = ...), such as an arc share. Parallel work on a function's own data belongs in @all or @scope, which run on worker threads too.

lora 
use arc;
use thread;

export fn main() void = {
	let hits = arc::new(thread::atomic { ... })!;
	let t = thread::spawn_with(arc::share(&hits), fn(h: arc::arc[thread::atomic]) void = {
		thread::add(arc::get(&h), 1);
	})!;
	thread::join(t);
	assert(thread::load(arc::get(&hits)) == 1);
}
lora 
use thread;
export fn main() void = {
	let n = 0;
	let p = &n;
	let t = thread::spawn(fn() void = { *p = 1; })!; // error: A thread may outlive `p`, which is a *int, a view of memory it doesn't own: it takes only what it owns.
	thread::join(t);
}

Coroutines run on one worker take turns (workers = 1), but the compiler can't know how many workers run them: mark such sharing unsafe { ... }, which vouches for it (unsafe code).

lora 
use coro;

fn bump(p: *int) void = { *p += 1; }
fn work(p: *int) void = bump(p);

export fn main() void = {
	let n = 0;
	let p = &n;
	@all(work(p), work(p))!; // error: `p` reaches data (an int) that may change while another thread uses it.
}
lora 
use coro;

fn work(p: *int) void = { *p += 1; }

export fn main() void = {
	let n = 0;
	let p = &n;
	@scope {
		@go work(p); // error: `p` reaches data (an int) that may change while another thread uses it.
		n += 1;
	}!;
}

Children may share what they only read, and each may have data of its own; results come back through @all:

lora 
use coro;

fn sum(xs: []const int) int = {
	let t = 0;
	for (let x .. xs) t += x;
	return t;
}

export fn main() void = {
	let xs = [1, 2, 3, 4];
	let v: []const int = xs[..];
	let (a, b) = @all(sum(v[..2]), sum(v[2..]))!;
	assert(a + b == 10);
}

21. Stack overflow checking

Stacks have a fixed size with a guard page below, so using too much stack stops the program with a report saying which stack ran out. A frame larger than a page is entered a page at a time, so even a large one meets the guard page rather than stepping over it. The compiler estimates every function's stack use and reports code that would overflow:

Entry pointStack
main, @init, @fini8 MiB, whatever ulimit -s says
@all, @first and @scope children, coro::detach, coro::detach_with256 KiB
coro::detach_sized(n, …), coro::detach_with_sized(n, …)n, rounded up to 16 KiB
thread::spawn, coro::blocking512 KiB
lora 
use coro;

fn deep() int = {
	let buf: [300 * 1024]u8 = [0...];
	return @int(buf[0]);
}

export fn main() void = {
	@scope { @go deep(); }!; // error: This coroutine needs up to 302 KiB of stack, more than the 256 KiB it gets
}
lora 
use coro;

fn deep() int = {
	let buf: [300 * 1024]u8 = [0...];
	return @int(buf[0]);
}

export fn main() void = {
	coro::detach_sized(320 * 1024, fn() void = { deep(); })!;   // enough
	coro::run();
}
lora 
export fn main() void = { // error: This program's main needs up to 9217 KiB of stack
	let big: [9 * 1024 * 1024]u8 = [0...];
	big[0] = 1;
}
  • The branches of an if or a match, and the statements of a block, share their temporaries' space; a block's bindings keep theirs until it ends. A local whose address is taken keeps its space for the whole function, as does everything inside a loop.
  • Recursion is a warning (its depth has no bound) wherever it is reached from, main included, unless @depth bounds it.
  • main's 8 MiB is what every program gets: macOS programs are linked with that stack, and on Linux the runtime raises the stack limit to it as the program starts (and the programs it starts get the raised limit too). Where the hard limit is lower, the stack is that much smaller, and an overflow is still caught by its guard page.
  • Calls through function pointers and closures, and into C, are counted as 16 KiB.
  • The estimate errs on the high side: it is never less than the frame the compiler lays out, which the test suite checks for the whole library.

Bounded recursion: @depth

@depth(d, n) on a function says that its parameter d counts how deep its recursion is, and that it goes at most n calls deep. Every call that recurses passes d + 1 (or more); a call deeper than n aborts at run time. Its stack use is then known — n + 1 of its largest frame, plus the most any call out of the recursion needs — so it is checked like any other code:

lora 
type tree = struct { kids: []tree }

// how deep a tree goes; trees deeper than 64 abort
@depth(level, 64) fn height(t: *const tree, level: usize) usize = {
	let most = 0z;
	for (let k .. t.kids) {
		let h = height(&k, level + 1);
		if (h > most) most = h;
	}
	return most + 1;
}

export fn main() void = {
	let leaf = tree { kids = [] }
	assert(height(&leaf, 0) == 1);
}

Recursion through several functions works the same way, as long as each of them has @depth and each call between them passes the depth on: one deeper (d + 1), or as it is (d), as long as every way round the recursion has a call that goes one deeper. A depth is then the heaviest chain of frames between two such calls. A call that passes something else, or a way round with no call one deeper, is a warning: the depth would have no bound.

The depth parameter counts the depth and nothing else: a body that changes it, or takes its address, is warned of, as @depth can then no longer bound the recursion. Count anything else in a variable of its own.

Code reading untrusted input checks its own limit first and fails with an error of its own before @depth's abort can happen, as the library's JSON, pack and regex readers do.

Move large buffers to the heap with alloc, or give the coroutine a larger stack. The editor offers both as quick fixes.

22. Modules

Declarations are private to their module unless marked export. use imports one of the core library modules:

lora 
use fmt;                        // fmt::println
use s = strings;                // an alias: s::toupper
use strings::{has_prefix}      // just these names, unqualified

export fn main() void = {
	assert(s::has_suffix("lora", "ra"));
	assert(has_prefix("lora", "lo"));
	fmt::println("ok")!;
}
lora 
use strings::{has_prefix}
export fn main() void = {
	strings::toupper("a"); // error: `strings::toupper` is an unknown object
}
lora 
use strings;
export fn main() void = {
	strings::utf8_len(1); // error: `strings::utf8_len` is an unknown object
}
  • A use-list imports only the names listed, not the module's other names.
  • The files of a program form one module. Programs cannot define their own named modules: the use namespace holds the core library (lib/) and the runtime (rt).
  • The core library's modules are listed in docs/stdlib.md.

23. Attributes

AttributeApplies toEffect
@initfunctionruns before main
@finifunctionruns after main returns
@testfunctiona test function (fn() / fn() (void | E) / fn(t: *testing::t) void)
@benchfunctiona benchmark function (fn(b: *testing::b) void) run with lora test --bench
@fuzzfunctiona fuzz target (fn(f: *testing::f) void) run with lora test --fuzz
@depth(n, max)functionbounds recursion depth statically for stack checking
@bits(T)structbitstruct packed into unsigned integer T (u8–u64)
@symbol("name")function, globalthe linker symbol: declares a C function or exports under a C name
@threadlocalglobalone copy per thread
@shorthand(name)typea tag type's short form (tags)
@rule(fn)typewhat checks a tag type's uses at compile time (tags)
@synchronisedglobalits module guards it for threads itself, as with a lock (data races)
@unsafefunction, interface methodits callers make sure of what it needs, in unsafe code; its body may do unsafe operations (unsafe code)
@uncheckedfunction, block, expressionno bounds checks inside, which makes it unsafe code: @unchecked { ... }, @unchecked a[i]
@inlinefunction, callits calls are replaced by its body; at a call, @inline f(x) replaces that one
@noinlinefunctionnever inlined
@partialmatch@partial match (x) { ... }: cases may be left out, and do nothing
@packedstructno padding between fields
@align(n)struct, unionaligned to n
@field_align(min = n, max = m)struct, unioneach field aligned to between n and m
@simplestruct, unioncompared as its bytes
@sealedstruct, unionits fields are its module's alone (layout)

@inline is always done, or it is an error that says why: a function that calls itself, makes a closure, has an ensures, takes variadic arguments, or uses something private to another module can't be. The inlined body behaves exactly as the call would, its defers and drops included. Inlining stops after 8 levels of @inline functions calling each other, and makes a call there instead.

@partial match does nothing for the cases it leaves out, so it has no value, and it can't leave out an error, which would be ignored without a word: handle errors with an arm of their own.

@unchecked removes bounds checks from indexing and slicing. An index out of range then reads or writes memory it shouldn't, so it is unsafe code, and the author's to get right.

Tags

A tag is a typed constant on a struct field, which a library defines and reads while compiling. A tag type is an ordinary struct, and @shorthand(name) gives it a short form. @name(...) is exactly a struct literal of it: positional arguments set its fields in order, name = value sets that field, and a bare field name sets a bool field to true.

lora 
export @shorthand(limit) type limit = struct {
	low: int = 0,
	high: int = 100,
	strict: bool = false,
}

type reading = struct {
	@limit(0, 10) level: int,                 // low = 0, high = 10
	@limit(high = 5, strict) count: int,
	@tag(limit { low = 1 }) rate: int,        // the long form
	other: int,
}

// A generator: expanded once per field, while compiling
fn valid[T](v: *const T) bool = {
	@for (f .. @fields(T)) {
		@if (@has_tag(f, limit)) {
			let t = @tag_of(f, limit);
			if (v.@(f) < t.low || v.@(f) > t.high) return false;
		}
	}
	return true;
}

export fn main() void = {
	let r = reading { level = 3, count = 5, rate = 1, other = -9 }
	assert(valid(&r));
	r.level = 11;
	assert(!valid(&r));
}

An unknown tag is an error, so a typo is never ignored:

lora 
export @shorthand(limit) type limit = struct { high: int = 100 }

type reading = struct {
	@limti(5) level: int, // error: @limti is an unknown tag
}

export fn main() void = void;

In a generator, @for (f .. @fields(T)) expands its body once per named field: f.name is the field's name, f.type its type, and x.@(f) that field of x. @if is a compile-time branch, and the branch not taken is not checked. @same(A, B), @kind(T), @owns(T), @borrows(T) (whether a value of T may view memory it doesn't own), @cycles(T), @has_zero(T), @implements(T, I), @sealed(T) (whether T is another module's @sealed type, whose fields only that module reads), @has_tag(f, tag) and @tag_of(f, tag) are constants, and @error("...") is a compile error when expanded. Tags emit nothing into the program, and are not in @typeinfo: generated code is direct field code, and an untagged type costs nothing. Tags are part of a struct's type, so two structs that differ only in tags are different, though @T(x) converts between them.

A generator that walks into the fields of whatever it is given asks @sealed(T) first, as another module's sealed type has fields it may not read:

lora 
use rt;
use time;

fn counted[T](v: *const T) usize = {
	@if (@kind(T) == rt::type_kind::STRUCT && !@sealed(T)) {
		let n = 0z;
		@for (f .. @fields(T)) {
			n += 1;
		}
		return n;
	} else {
		return 1; // a whole: its fields are its module's
	}
}

type pair = struct { a: int, b: int }

export fn main() void = {
	assert(counted(&pair { a = 1, b = 2 }) == 2);
	assert(counted(&time::now()) == 1);
}

@rule(fn) on a tag type names a function run at compile time for each struct using the tag, so a bad tag is an error at the field even if nothing reads it. See config and json in the standard library, and docs/tags.md for the rules in full.

An example of attributes

lora 
use fmt;

let ready = false;

@init fn setup() void = { ready = true; }
@fini fn teardown() void = fmt::println("bye")!;

export fn main() void = { assert(ready); }

24. Calling C

Declare a C function with @symbol and no body, and call it in unsafe { ... }: C doesn't follow Lora's rules, so the compiler can't check the call. C strings are *const u8: make one with strings::cstr, which gives an owned NUL-terminated copy, and pass &c[0]:

lora 
use strings;

@symbol("abs") fn c_abs(x: i32) i32;
@symbol("strlen") fn c_strlen(s: *const u8) usize;
@symbol("snprintf") fn snprintf(buf: *u8, n: usize, format: *const u8, ...) int;

export fn main() void = {
	assert(unsafe { c_abs(-4) } == 4);
	let c = strings::cstr("hello")!;
	assert(unsafe { c_strlen(&c[0]) } == 5);
	let buf: [32]u8 = [0...];
	let f = strings::cstr("%d")!;
	unsafe { snprintf(&buf[0], len(buf), &f[0], 42) }
	assert(buf[0] == @u8('4'));
}

Lora functions can be implemented with C variadics too:

lora 
fn total(n: int, ...) int = {
	let ap = vastart();
	defer vaend(ap);
	let t = 0;
	for (let i = 0; i < n; i += 1) t += vaarg(ap, int);
	return t;
}

export fn main() void = { assert(total(3, 1, 2, 3) == 6); }
  • export fn with @symbol("name") gives C code a Lora function to call.
  • A str cannot be cast to *u8: it is not NUL-terminated.
  • Limit: passing or returning structs of 16 bytes or less by value to or from C does not follow the C ABI (a QBE limit). Pass pointers to them instead.
  • C cannot call closures; only capture-free lambdas and functions convert to *fn.

25. Unit functions

A function can state what it needs and what it promises, which makes it a unit function. requires(condition) is checked when the function is entered; ensures(condition) when it returns. They go after the result type, before the body:

lora 
fn divide(dividend: int, divisor: int) int
	requires(divisor != 0)
= dividend / divisor;

fn absolute(n: int) int
	requires(n != -2147483648, "the smallest int has no absolute value")
	ensures(r => r >= 0)
= if (n < 0) -n else n;

export fn main() void = {
	assert(divide(9, 3) == 3 && absolute(-4) == 4);
}
  • ensures(r => condition) names the value returned r; ensures(condition) names nothing. Several may follow each other, and each may have a message after a comma, which may be $"...".
  • When. All requires run in order on entry. All ensures run in order on every return, after the function's defers, so they see its final result. A function that returns an error skips its posts, and r is the success part of the result: ensures(r => r > 0) on (int | error) reads an int.
  • Lambdas take them the same way: fn(x: int) int requires(x < 1000) = x * 2.
  • Interfaces. requires and ensures on an interface's method hold for every impl, through the interface or not, in any module. An impl may add posts but not pres: code written against the interface only knows the interface's. Its parameters keep the interface's names, which the conditions use, and the conditions mean what they meant where the interface was written: their names are that module's, even private ones.
  • Generic functions check them in every instance.
  • C functions. A function without a body, with an @symbol, may have them too: the compiler makes a function of that name which checks them around the call.
  • assert(condition[, message]) in a body is checked the same way: reported the same way and seen by the same handler.

A condition only looks: it can't assign to anything but its own variables, allocate or free memory, return (an error passed on with ?, say), defer, or move or make an owner. An ensures can't read a parameter that owns memory or that the function changes, since it would not see what was passed:

lora 
fn bump(n: int) int ensures(r => r == n + 1) = { // error: An ensures clause can't read `n`, which the function changes (or takes the address of): it would not see the value passed
	n += 1;
	return n;
}

export fn main() void = void;

Checked at compile time. A call whose arguments are all constants, to a function of any module, breaks its requires then and there; so does any condition during compile-time execution:

lora 
fn half(n: int) int requires(n % 2 == 0) = n / 2;

export fn main() void = {
	let h = half(7); // error: This call breaks what half requires: n % 2 == 0
}

A false condition is a bug, not an error to handle, so ? never sees it, unless the result type has unit::error (below). By default the program stops with a report naming the condition, where it is, and for a requires, that the caller broke it:

text 
main.lora:4:2: abort: divide requires divisor != 0 (so the code calling divide broke it): its caller passed a value where that's false.

rt::on_unit_failure(&handler) replaces the report with a function of yours, given an rt::unit_failure: its kind (REQUIRES, ENSURES or ASSERT), function, predicate (as written), message, path, line and column. The program stops once the handler returns, unless it was built to observe; the handler may also exit itself.

Build modes, lora run --units=<mode> (or lora build, or LORA_UNITS=<mode>), for the files given:

ModeA false condition
enforce (the default, in every build)is reported, and the program stops
observeis reported, and the program carries on
ignoreis not checked: requires and ensures are not evaluated

Since conditions only look, ignoring them changes nothing else. assert still runs in ignore builds, and stops the program, as what its condition does may be needed: assert(set::add(&seen, x)?).

Waiting: @expect. requires and ensures are checked once. Something that becomes true later is waited for with a block that runs again until it succeeds:

lora 
use unit;

type screen = (int | str);

fn focus() screen = "the cart";

fn cart() (str | unit::error) = {
	return @expect(within = 2000, every = 50) {
		let name = focus() as str;
		assert(name != "");
		yield name;
	}
}

export fn main() void = {
	assert(cart()! == "the cart");
}

  • A false assert, a failed as, or an error from ? in the block ends the attempt, and it runs again after every milliseconds, 50 if not given. The block's own defers run, and its owners are dropped. Other failures are as anywhere: x! and a false requires of a function it calls still stop the program. So does an assert inside a lambda or defer in the block.

  • within is required, and is in milliseconds, as any integer. With none left, or a negative one, there is one attempt and no waiting. When it has passed, the function returns unit::expectation_failed, with what the last attempt saw: the values an assert compared, what an as found, or the error a ? got. So @expect needs unit::error in the result (L1002, L1003).

    text 
    open: expected d.id == id, after 2000 ms: d.id is 2, id is 1
open: expected detail, after 2000 ms: it is loading { left = 3 }
open: expected no error, after 2000 ms: cannot fetch /items: code 503

    Each side of && counts as its own assert, so the report says which was false. Each side of a comparison runs once per attempt.

  • Its value is what the block yields, and it may do I/O: unlike a condition, it is ordinary code that runs again.

  • It always runs, in ignore builds too, but not in @comptime. In a coroutine it waits with coro::sleep, so that others keep running; otherwise it sleeps the thread.

  • It is not a loop: break and continue can only leave it for a loop named around it.

  • A message in it is a plain str, for the same reason as below.

A failure can be a result. The result type decides. With unit::error in it, a false requires or ensures is returned, for the caller to handle like any other error:

lora 
use unit;

type account = struct { cents: i64 }

fn withdraw(a: *account, cents: i64) (i64 | unit::error)
	requires(cents > 0, "the amount must be positive")
	requires(cents <= a.cents)
	ensures(r => r >= 0)
= {
	a.cents -= cents;
	return a.cents;
}

export fn main() void = {
	let a = account { cents = 100 }
	assert(withdraw(&a, 40)! == 60);
	assert((withdraw(&a, 500) or 0i64) == 0);
	assert(a.cents == 60); // the body did not run
}

Printed, the failure reads withdraw requires cents <= a.cents, followed by its message if it has one. A false requires returns before the body; a false ensures returns after it and its defers, in place of the value it returned. Nothing is reported, no handler runs, and a call with constant arguments is not a compile error. Build modes do not apply, in ignore builds too: a failure that is a result is how the function works, and its caller is handling it.

Because it returns, it can't lose an owner: a false ensures would drop an owner the function returned, and a false requires one passed to it, so with unit::error both are compile errors (L1000). The message must be a plain str, not $"...", as the failure holds it (L1001).

26. Defined behaviour

Every operation in Lora has a defined result, the same on every machine, at run time and in compile-time evaluation. When an operation cannot give a meaningful result, the program stops and says why, where, and with what values; nothing is left to chance.

WhatResult
integer overflow, i32::MAX + 1aborts with the values (a constant one is a compile error); +% -% *% wrap
x / -1, x % -1-x (MIN / -1 overflows), 0
division or remainder by zeroaborts (a constant one is a compile error)
shift by the width or more, or a negative countaborts saying so (a constant one is a compile error)
float to integer, @i32(f)saturates; NaN is 0
an index or slice out of rangeaborts with the index and the length
alloc, append or insert of more bytes than an address can countnomem: the slice is as it was, never smaller than it says
a value outside a pattern type, @port(70000)aborts with the value and the pattern
a value no match arm coversaborts saying so
an operator on a tagged union, (int | void) > 0a compile error: take the member out first
x! on an erroraborts with the error, its notes and its trace
a false requires, ensures or assertaborts naming the condition (unit functions)
a variable before it is set (@undefined)zero; a compile error for a type zero is not a value of
mixing number types, i64 + i32, or passing a u8 as a u64a compile error: convert with @T(x)
an error kept in a variable nothing reads, or dropped by _ =>a compile error (L0003, L0006)
memory: leaks, use after free, double free, dangling stack pointersowners make them impossible; raw memory is checked as described in Memory, through calls and copies too
a data race: threads changing shared data at oncea compile error, unless the data is thread-safe (data races)

Unsafe code

Lora's unsafe operations are converting between unrelated pointer types or from an integer (@*T(x)), indexing or slicing a [*]T array, which has no length, calling C, calling an @unsafe function, and managing raw memory (release, adopt, free of what no owner holds). Each needs unsafe { ... }, where its author vouches for it:

lora 
@symbol("abs") fn c_abs(x: i32) i32;

export fn main() void = {
	let x = 7;
	let n = unsafe { c_abs(-4) }         // C
	let p = unsafe { @*[*]u8(&x) }      // a raw view of x's bytes
	let first = unsafe { p[0] }          // no bounds check
	assert(n == 4 && first == 7);
}

unsafe { a; b; value } gives its last expression, written without a ;. It is not contagious: a safe function may hold an unsafe block. What an unsafe block stores and shares is vouched for too: pointers it keeps are not checked for dangling, nor what it changes for data races. A block must hold something unsafe: one that holds nothing unsafe is an error (L0801), so each one marks code to read with care. The runtime, rt, is Lora's trusted base, where unsafe operations are allowed throughout.

An @unsafe function needs something of its callers that the compiler can't check, such as a pointer to a value of some type, or a lock held: its comment says what. Calling it is an unsafe operation, and so is taking it as a function value, which could be called anywhere. Its body is unsafe code. A function that checks what it needs itself is safe, however unsafe its body: it holds unsafe { ... } blocks, and is not @unsafe:

lora 
@symbol("abs") fn c_abs(x: i32) i32;

// The bytes of v, which must be a value of n bytes at least.
@unsafe fn bytes_of(v: *opaque, n: usize) []u8 = (@*[*]u8(v))[..n];

// Safe: it gives the right length itself.
fn first_byte(x: *u64) u8 = unsafe { bytes_of(x, size_of(u64)) }[0];

export fn main() void = {
	let x = 7u64;
	assert(first_byte(&x) == 7);
	assert(unsafe { c_abs(-2) } == 2);
}

An interface's method can be @unsafe too, when what it needs is the caller's to make sure of: memory given back to the allocator it came from, say. Calling it, through the interface or on a type that implements it, is an unsafe operation, and each impl of it is @unsafe as well, since its body relies on the same thing. An impl's method can't be @unsafe where the interface's is not: callers through the interface would not know.

lora 
type store = interface {
	fn get() int;
	// n must be a value this store gave
	@unsafe fn give_back(n: int) void;
};

type cell = struct { v: int };

impl store for cell {
	fn get(c: *cell) int = c.v;
	@unsafe fn give_back(c: *cell, n: int) void = { c.v -= n; };
};

export fn main() void = {
	let c = cell { v = 5 };
	let s: store = &c;
	let n = s.get();
	unsafe { s.give_back(n) };
	assert(s.get() == 0);
}

A raw pointer used wrongly in unsafe code, such as a null or freed one, or a stack that overflows through deep recursion, is reported rather than silent:

text 
abort: null pointer dereference (address 0x0): a raw pointer that was null was used
abort: stack overflow: the main stack (8192 KiB) ran out, likely through deep or endless recursion
abort: stack overflow: a coroutine's stack (256 KiB) ran out, likely through deep or endless recursion; coro::detach_sized gives one more

27. What Lora does not have

MissingUse instead
Exceptionserror types with ? and ! (§10)
Garbage collection, borrow checkingalloc/free and defer, with leak checks (§12)
Classes, inheritance, methods outside implstructs, interfaces
Function and operator overloadingdistinct names, generics
switch, while, domatch, for (cond)
Nested named functionslambdas
String indexing and +strings::at, strings::concat, $"..."
== on structs, arrays, tuples, tagged unionscompare fields; match
Constant generic parameters, several constraints, default type argumentsslices; one constraint per parameter
User-defined named modulesone program module; core library modules
Hardware SIMD intrinsicsvectors module for fixed-width lane vectors; native SIMD codegen planned
